body: We had really high hopes for this place, and even though we did see turtles we were concerned how disruptive the staff were to the turtles and how many people were allowed to crowd round them. The guides kept saying the nest had “collapsed” and multiple turtles were making their way back to sea which we now believe after researching it was due to high levels of disruption from guides constantly checking and shining lights to see if they were in the egg laying process. In the group there was maybe 50/60 people and people were allowed to crowd round the turtle. We left after we saw a turtle laying eggs and noticed one of the guides was holding the back leg/flipper out the way. We truly do not believe this place is ethical what so ever and we’re disappointed we paid 4000 lkr to join the turtle watch. We absolutely would avoid in the future and wouldn’t recommend. We have never wrote a bad review and are very fair people, but this one was 100% justified. There are lots of young tourists who absolutely do not care about turtles or their welfare.
title: I wouldn’t recommend unfortunately

body: I read a number of reviews and it is obvious that now Sri Lanka is relatively calm after decades of different challenges the tourist numbers have increased significantly. This is apparent in number of hotels being constructed in the area Rekawa Beach is protected as it is a major turtle nesting beach and there are improvements since we were last here in 2023.Firslty during turtle nesting season you are not allowed on the beach between 1900 hrs and 0600 hrs unless you are accompanied by an official guide.Secondly there are now 10 rangers employed overnight who can target the turtle nesting location.This is essential so they can relocate the laid eggs in a restricted area where they are reburied and sand covered in mesh.The hatching can be estimated by the gestation period.During the day this restricted area is under surveillance by two rangers.The turtle egg relocation is to ensure that the iguanas do not eat the eggs.One of the images shows an iguana at egg burial site.The hotels do not necessarily promote night turtle watching from a conservation perspective and to not disturb the turtles,Obviously there is a financial element to guided turtle watching and the reviews suggest that the behaviour in these groups is sometimes unruly but this is human nature particulary in instagram age.We were fortunate to observe under guidance a turtle laying eggs during daylight late afternoon.It was quite extraordinary and at a similar time another day we observed hatching olive turtles both by accident as we were doing a walk on the expansive beachDuring our early morning daily walks on the beach you could observe all the turtle tracks.It must be a challenging journey as there are strong undercurrents huge crashing waves creating steep access in parts.It is also totally unsuitable beach for swimming
title: Improved protection for turtles nesting

body: We visited this sea turtle conservation centre, expecting to see a place that is really about animal welfare and real conservation. Unfortunately, our experience has been very disappointing.It seemed to be more of a money-driven business than a real turtle conservation project. The main thing they offer visitors is to pick up turtles and take pictures. It looked unethical and nothing like animal welfare.There was little information on the actual protection of turtles or the educational part. We were expecting to learn more about conservation and see real animal care, but instead it looked like a tourist attraction for photographs.A very disappointing experience.
title: Frustration is more like a way to make money.

body: This was a very interesting experience.We arrived just 8pm. We waited for an hour and then were taken to the beach. It was about a 20 minute walk to where the turtles are. There were about 40 people in the group but we were divided into sub- groups to step forward to see the turtle laying her eggs. Everyone was very respectful and the guides organised everything very well. On the walk back we saw 2 turtles making their way back to the sea.I was unsure beforehand if I really wanted to go in this trip but on balance I think it was worth it.The unknown factor of course is who else is in the group.The money from this activity means that the villagers protect the turtles rather than taking their eggs to sell.
title: An interesting experience.

body: We walked in to get some information about how the activity works, so we could decide for ourselves whether we wanted to do it. After a guide gave a non-obligatory introduction and we read the information boards about the turtles, we still had some doubts. When we started to walk away to take a shower at our nearby hotel first, the guide asked where we were going and why we weren’t buying a ticket. This made us decide not to return, as it felt to us that the turtles were being used as a money-making attraction for the center. Luckily, earlier that afternoon we had already seen a baby turtle on the beach while taking a walk.
title: Money comes first, turtles second

body: We really enjoyed the experience, everything was explained to us at the start and within 90 minutes we were led to the beach to see baby turtles hatching and paddling towards the beach. Everyone was respectful and kept their distance in what was a magical experience

body: Having read other reviews before we visited this place I have chosen to include a review to “balance the perspective” a little. My wife and I paid a visit to this community conservation project with a little trepidation because of other reviews. However, our experience was one whereby nature was given the respect of those organising the “turtle watch” and they did so in a way which didn’t cause distress to the turtle mum we saw laying her eggs that night. We also saw babies making their way to the ocean (unusual for November apparently)These guys are responsible for a 4km stretch of beach which is designated protected and closed to the public 7pm to 7am and are protecting these endangered animals with the money they raise from visitors (LKR 2,000 per head) plus donations received so should be supported. We were only asked to walk 500 metres but depending on the activity you might need to walk up to 4kms to see anything. The “rules of attendance” are clearly explained to people in advance and throughout but if our experience is anything to go by there is always some idiot who chooses not to obey the rules or lets their children run around uncontrolled despite being pulled up about it repeatedly. Overall a magical opportunity to see and help an endangered species survive providing you follow the guidelines given.
title: Save the turtles…..

body: What should have been the most beautiful experience ruined by impatient tourists. Sadly I would not recommend this experience. Not because of the beautiful nature you might see. More that people don’t know how to behave properly anymore.We turned up at 8:15 pm. We were the second group ( of 2) Group 1 before us had only 2 people in it also.There were 8 groups. This is clearly too much for humans to abide by these days . Phones lighting up constantly playing games or on Facebook. The guide saying NO LIGHT.Finally when we could go to see the turtle lay . Group 1 was called. Remember this was 2 people. Nope 30 rude impatient tourists of all nationalities pushed forward. So much so that they ruined their own chances of a peaceful life experience.Same again , group 2. My group of just me and my wife . Bundled by 30 more. Group 3 with children, nope pushed out the way for photo grabbing moments. The worst of humanity came out on the most beautiful night of nature.It was not policed by the guides . Why should it be . The moment they catch the wave and disappear is just magic. We were very lucky and the project is definitely worth the support and the entry donation.

body: A really memorable experience, well-curated by the local guide, who took trouble to ensure that everyone had a good chance to see these remarkable creatures, while minimising disturbance to them. It seems like a very worthwhile and important contribution to the long-term protection and preservation of several large turtle species. We'd recommend highly - and applaud the work of the teams who scour the beach to protect against poaching and other threats to the eggs. Alas, we saw monitor lizards digging up the freshly-laid egg clutches the following morning - but this is nature at its rawest, and has clearly been going on since the dawn of time. A great experience and a good cause: well worth supporting, from all that we saw.
title: Great experience and a worthy conservation cause too

body: These guys are doing a great job against all odds. Local pollution, fishing nets , locals stealing hatchings and stray dogs feeding the young. Please support them. Numbers have increased slightly so their is not in vain. We saw a huge green turtle laying her eggs at midnight under a full moon. An unforgettable experience. Thank you Tushan, we will be back to support you more

body: We've done turtle watching before in places like Costa Rica and South America. And while no one can predict how the turtle watching will be (we saw two different turtles laying eggs here), the organization for watching those turtles could be significantly improved. In our case, we had to hike 2 kilometers each direction, in the dark, without lights to find the turtle they wanted us to see. The original turtle that we came to see was about 100 meters away, in the dark, under a bush without any red lights available. For all I knew, my mother was under that tree laying eggs!! Obviously, a complete bust. Thankfully, we encountered one along the beach as we were walking back to the meeting point and here, we could actual see something. The "director" of the facility kept telling us "100 more metres" and we couldn't walk on the compressed sand, only the soft sand....so it was completely un-enjoyable. While the laying of the eggs was okay, it was a single turtle and after 3.5 hrs, I had enough and walked back. Definitely would not do again. You want to see turtles laying eggs? Go to Costa Rica!!

body: It was an amazing experience to see how these incredible animals continue their life cycle. It has been difficult with increasing human population, pollution, destruction of natural habitats, and climate change. Only 1 in 1000 survive to become an adult turtle. 5 out of 7 turtle verities come to this small area of protected beach in Rekawa, and the stuff here work so hard to protect them in their natural habitat. We were lucky to see 2 fully grown green turtles (over 1 meter). The entire process takes about 2 to 3 hours, from the point coming out from the sea to go back. If you come to the centre around 8.30 pm, you can get a ticket and join the tours (make sure you had dinner, we were too uninformed to think it is about an hour 🤣🤣) #turtles #greenturtle #rekawaturtlewatch #rekawabeach
title: Amazing experience - Rekawa turtle watch

body: This is just one of those amazing experiences, that will live with me and my wife, for as long as we live..BUT...!!!We love conservation work..We absolutely like the idea of volunteers trying to not just help species of this planet but protect species from people who just want to poach or destroy a species....And if, as we did, it takes many hours of one's time waiting around for the signal to follow someone in darkness, along a long beach, with just a red light to guide us, and once at location, wait maybe another hour to get chance too finally take a picture under said red light, and be part of a Green Turtle's time on a beach, digging hole too lay her Eggs, absolutely fine by us..Now...!!!If you're the type of person with no patience, no care, and no understanding or respect of nature, then please do NOT go here..There is a nominal fee of around £4.25..per person..And they just hope a contribution is given after your experience..They operate solely on donations to keep up this valuable work..There are laminated cards with explanation of everything in many many languages to help understand the work these people do..It was around 4hrs in total for us, from arriving, the talk about the turtles , getting to experience what we saw, and getting back to starting point..If you love nature and you're interested in conservation work , you will enjoy this experience..But if you're not interested in what is actually being offered here, then simply don't turn up..Because this experience is about wildlife..And wildlife by the very nature, don't turn up at the beach when you want or expect them too..Thoroughly enjoyed our magical moments tonight..During our time on the beach,where around 12 of us mingled, we also saw fireflies and fluorescent plankton flowing onto the beach...

body: We visited this evening and had high hopes. When we arrived the information centre was pretty good with some interesting facts etc., there were a small handful of people there which we thought was a good sized group. But then many more tourists arrived totally around 50 odd people and we had no briefing from the guide (in his defence he did not speak much English). After waiting for the call that a turtle was digging on the beach to lay her eggs, everyone was rushed into the centre to pay 1000 rupees each (fairly reasonable price) and then everyone was marched into the darkness along a track and onto the beach by the guide (quite rough terrain in some areas). We then walked/power walked up the beach and spotted two hatchlings trying to make it down to the water, the guide didn't seem that concerned that 50 pairs of human feet were stampeding through the sand in total darkness, potentially crushing other hatchlings trying to make it alive (nobody was provided with infrared torches, only the guide had one and he was marching on way ahead of the group - you're not allowed to use your phone light to ensure the turtles are not disturbed but in this way nobody knew whether they were crushing baby turtles in the sand!!). After about a 1km walk we reached the area of the large female, we waited for approx 1 hr to ensure she had made her chamber (this was fine to wait), but during this time everyone was talking loud and flashing their phones everywhere potentially disturbing the female). Once she started egg laying everyone was hoarding round her and it felt very instrusive - the guide said 10 people at a time but as there was only one guide to 50 people crowd control was tough, so what you get is too many people getting far too close and disturbing the turtle too much, people's flash going off causing more disturbance... At this point we decided to leave early as we didn't want to play a part any more.Also an elderly gentlemen was left behind at the start because the guide was marching off up the beach, he was pretty upset at being left in the darkness on his own - understandably!!This project has good intentions put really poor organisation which results in poor regard for animal welfare... An English speaking guide and smaller group size is desperately needed to ensure welfare and minimise disturbance. I could not recommend this to anyone who loves wildlife, the project needs great improvement and whilst it was amazing to see a turtle, we couldn't enjoy it due to rowdy tourists who care more about snapping a picture than minimising disturbance. Avoid!!!
title: Uncomfortable...

body: I just want to write about my experience here two nights ago: Jan 30th. I feel so guilty,disgusted and ashamed that I was there. My guide who does safaris suggested we go last minute as he had not seen it before and was curious as he is really into animals, nature and wildlife. There was only a couple of people there at the start which I thought was fine. You are given a briefing at the start about staying behind the turtle and no flash photography etc. They have someone down at the beach watching for a turtle and then they alert you. Gradually more and more people showed up and there was a crowd of at least 30 people. The guide reminded everyone to change their camera settings and that he did not want to here sorry after a flash went off as the damage would be done. Then we walked about 1km up the beach. Then everyone gathered right up around the turtle in the sand with no gap forming a circle around her while she panted laying her eggs. I stood far back as I thought we were to be at least 2 metres away and it seemed horrible on the turtle to be so close. Then out of nowhere a n extremely rude tourist couple arrived with children from a shortcut maybe as they were too mean to pay the costs to get in. The parents were really loud and the mother walked over with her 2 kids right bedside the turtle and immediately used her camera with flash to photograph the turtleneck . Even if I had not been told not to do this I would have known it was wrong. The kids were being very noisy too again not their fault they were probably over tired given the time of night. Very selfish of anyone to bring their children their at this time as it is the parents who do not want to miss out on this touristic experience. The children I saw were too young to appreciate it even if this was an okay thing to do. Then I witnessed the guide physically touching the turtle mother by patting her with his hands while she tried to lay the eggs and dig the sandpit,that was a complete disgrace. I said to my guide I wanted to go then as I was very upset and the whole thing was disgusting so we left . Apparently the group stays on for much longer while eggs are layed etc. I had enough. It really is a shocking thing to be happening especially with the world as it is today. We are destroying everything and nothing with nature is sacred anymore not even a mama turtle laying her hatchlings. Do not support this terrible organisation and I don't care if local people are making a living out of it, it's wrong. The sri lankan government needs to stop this immediately and anyone who goes after reading this should seriously question their judgement.
title: DO NOT GO TO THIS!!NEEDS TO BE STOPPED IMMEDIATELY

body: I have always loved seeing turtles in their natural habitat and it's always been a dream to see hatchlings run back to the sea, so when we found out that you could witness this through a professional conservation project in Tangalle, I was so excited!We arrived around 9pm - there were around 15-20 people already waiting. The guide announced a turtle had been spotted on the beach starting to lay her eggs - so we made our way down.The guide mentioned no flash lights were to be used as these disturb the turtles and we much remain quiet whilst observing the process.When we arrived near the turtle, the guide broke us off into small groups of about 8 people and one group at a time we approached to witness the turtle laying her eggs whilst respecting nature and staying only behind the turtle with just the red lights from the guides to see - this was so magical to experience, the turtle was around 1metre long and we saw atleast 5 eggs being laid. After a few moments the guide moved us along for the next small group to approach.A few moments later, 40+ people stormed the beach. The tour guides must of called other operators in the area to tell them where the turtle was, or a late tour bus had turned up at the centre - this is where the experience turned incredibly sour and upsetting.The crowds were uncontrollable - atleast 20 people surrounded the turtle at a time, taking photos with their flash on and we even saw children throwing sand at the turtle - it was disgusting that parents weren't controlling their children and the guides did nothing to stop this either.We sat on the sidelines for around another 10 minutes whilst people crowded the turtle, talking loudly with children screeching. Guides mentioned an few times to not use the flashes but the crowds were so large they just ignored them.This was so distressing to watch that poor turtle become a performing monkey whilst giving birth to her eggs.. ignorant uneducated people disturbing nature and NOTHING being done by the guides to ensure a calm environment for the animal.We felt disgusted that this was being allowed to happen to that poor turtle so after a few attempts to tell the crowds to "shh", we left. Feeling guilty and so sad.If you love these animals.. do NOT go and disturb them during this process. You can swim off any of the beaches on the south coast of Sri Lanka and see them in their natural habitat. I so so wish you will read this and respect these animals...
title: Uncontrollable ignorant tourist disturbing nature..

title: Excellent experience

body: At this point of time I was lucky to be in a group of only maybe 9 people (after the Colombo bombings tourist numbers have decreased significantly) high seasons can get up to 20-30 more 😓The conservation is a small house at the gateway to Rawaka Beach - the 4 or 5 male staff were all INCREDIBLY rude as stated in many other previous reviews and with no introduction or information on the turtles. All 9 tourists just at this small run centre for 2.5 hours until one of the men came with his red flash touch and said “come” we all followed. Walking far along the beach maybe 15 minutes until we came across only 1 large green turtle still attempting to dig her nest. We all gathered around her nest with the one red light - couple of imbeciles(as you would expect) accidentally used their flash and some accidentally shining their bright screens on the poor turtle. Phones should be BANNED completely, I can’t stress enough some tourists have no brains and are so obsessed in taking a photo it’s ridiculous. Watching her dig she then stopped and headed back to the sea! This was INCREDIBLY SAD and HEARTBREAKING that she didn’t lay her eggs. I’m not sure why? Maybe we had scared her? or the bright phone lights?There was no schedule which is needed, strict guidelines and rules need to be placed on tourists!!! I have no idea where the 1000 rupees go because something needs to changed here along with professionalism. Overall I deeply regret visiting this beach I left feeling unfulfilled and deeply saddened as I feel like I had witnessed a fall in nature because humans had obstructed it’s natural course. 😔
title: LEAVING EXPERIENCE SAD AND GUILTY💔

body: We were staying in the villa on the beach and could see the turtle so we stepped down on the beach from the property with our red lights once the ranger had approached. He had one red light for approx 20 people that were with him! The turtle had already laid her eggs. We stood and watched for 5 minutes and it was amazing to experience but the weather was bad and we had children with us so we went back up the steps to our accommodation. Despite the stormy conditions the Ranger appeared charged us $15 for stepping onto the beach - we don't mind paying for a service that is going to a good cause - it just felt a little excessive as didn't actually get a guide, no information - just a very brief peak of a turtle covering her eggs for 5 minutes. In Hikkaduwa we saw plenty of turtles freely coming up onto the beach.
title: Not sure about this one!

body: The turtle watching begins at approximately 8.30pm each evening. It was really interesting visiting the conservation centre while we waited to set off to the beach. The guides were informative and clearly put the interest of the turtles first (We were a little apprehensive in case it was a touristy gimmick and interfered with the turtles’ natural behaviour which it didn’t seem to do) We were amazed to see a turtle in the nest she’d made at the back of the beach and covering her eggs. I wasn’t expecting to see it up so close and it was incredible. Later we watched tiny baby turtles all scuttle down to sea for the first time (must be careful not to tread on them in the dark!!) The highlight for me was later seeing the mum leave her nest and make the slow journey back down to sea. Awesome.
title: Incredible turtle watching experience

body: Though it is very special to see a turtle laying eggs I have mixed feelings. There were a lot of people, I think about 40. Everyone was standing around the turtle. I don’t think she could lay her eggs in a calm way.After the tourguide shouted that there was a nest hatching nearby. The group quickly walked to the place where dozens of hatchlings made their way to the see. Again, this was special to see but it felt weird with so many people around the babies. People could easily step on them because it was so dark and the babies were everywhere. So, in short, I hope they would regulate these tours more. Maybe Handle a maximum of people and don’t let them come too close to the animals. If you care fo animal welfare, don’t take the tour.
title: Mixed feelings

body: rekrekawa ch is one of the best quite bech in deep south,One of the best place to see turtles and laying eggs..nesting season start january to july, i saw 6 🐢 in between 400m, that was lovely and must see project..they charge for adults 1000rs,children from 6year 500rs which is going to staff salaries .if you dont see turtles at all they dont charge...
title: Dumi

body: WOW ...living in Sri Lanka for 17 years and visiting this beautiful island for 28 years this was my first experience of this very special programThe conservation program takes great care to provide the necessary information to ensure the turtles and eggs are not disturbed and protected. A MUST for any travel itinerary in Sri Lanka .... The community team also keeps the beach clean and protects the environment ...such a brilliant experience that will touch my heart forever ... can recommend staying at Green Turtle guest house which is less than 30 seconds walk from this program and Ruwani restaurant and coffee shop for dinner before this magical experience (only 5 minute walk)
title: A special community program to protect the turtles

body: When we arrived we paid and everyone walked to the beach. Pitch black, 12 people one guide. Not sure if we missed the introduction? But everyone looked as lost as us, walking and walking and walking in the dark. Guide didn’t help ‘guide’ people, he just walked off ahead with the one light. When we did find turtles it was pretty amazing to see them laying eggs, HOWEVER, not when the guide held the light right on her ass for 15 minutes and then grabbed one of her eggs and pressed it between his fingers to show how soft it was. AND then he literally jumped on top of her, to “help” free her from some branches that were on top of her, but he also then used his light to read her tag number, which was up near her face.... yet he never wrote it down, was this only for personal interest??All this while she is still trying to cover her eggs for safety... really!?!Couldn’t understand a word he was saying most the time, accent was really hard. I’m not normally this critically honestly, but come on guys sort this product out! Educate, show respect and above all SET an example! We are just the tourist after all... what do we know.
title: Abusing their privilege

body: I totally agree with Hobart. Very intrusive on the turtles, the guides themselves were standing way too close to the turtles while it’s nesting and speaking loudly, non of the recognized guidelines (other than the red lights) were followed. My guide even told me that tourists were allowed to touch the turtles, but I didn’t see that for myself.
title: Horrible experience

body: Very intrusive to the poor turtles laying eggs. Inconsiderate, rude tourists who got way too close to the turtles. Very poor explanation also. Wish we never went. My kids and I ended up leaving early after baby turtles were let out of a bag. Don't bother going if you like animals.
title: Don't bother

body: Knowledgeable guides, we saw a turtle laying/burying eggs and a baby turtle making his maiden voyage to the beach. So so great!!
title: AMAZING!!!!

body: I cannot recommend this completely. Upside: I liked seeing 2 green turtles, learned a lot and was amazed by their size. The guides were efficient to find the turtles. Unfortunately didn’t see them laying eggs: Turtle #1 building her chamber which collapsed so she had to find a new spot (by then we had to leave because of the security curfew) and Turtle #2 returning to the sea as she got scared by lightning. Downside: 1) Guide never answered my question about “when can we see the eggs hatch and take their walk to the sea”? I’m not sure what happens with the eggs. Some websites state that 100% of eggs in south west Lanka get sold 1) as delicacy or 2) to hatcheries.2) promised to have group of max 10 - we were about 20. 3) mobile phones or cameras should be forbidden. People just can’t follow the rule to NOT use lights and the rangers are not strict enough about it. Just enjoying the experience would be great. 4) in my opinion we got way too close and I wonder how much it stressed the turtle. Already hard enough to crawl in the sand with 120 eggs in the belly and then be chased by humans making the sand vibrate. Summary:It’s been a dream of mine to watch them lay eggs and hatch - both we didn’t see. Most worried about the eggs and the conversation part of the project.
title: What happens with the eggs?!

body: It was really great to see a majestic giant turtle laying eggs on the beach. However there were more than 50 people trying to see one turtle and little or no control. We felt annoyed at the lack of control which brought to mind the phrase "trying to herd cats". Our guide should have had some help trying to control the people on the beach. Too many people for one guy and probably too much disturbance for one turtle.
title: Like herding cats!

body: When we arrived he told us to have a look inside which had a load of information on turtles, it was interesting to read. He then told us the way it works is they have people on the beach scouting and when they have sight of turtles he gets a call and then we will go. After about 45 minutes of waiting (no problem) he gets everyone together (about 60 people) and we head towards the beach. It started off ok everyone in line, he told us to wait while he checked out the turtle, he went over to it and the turtle was laying eggs. We didn’t like the way he start breaking apart trees and bushes around it to expose the turtle whilst it was happening, we was told 10 at a time but everyone just seemed to run over and crowd the turtle, there was no control off the group. There were younger people (old enough to understand how to act appropriately) running half a mile down the shore line screaming and playing in the sea, bare in mind there was another turtle trying to come in land at the time which was probably very frightened and despite being told no lights or flash photography people felt the need to take photos with the flash which can blind the turtle. I was really disappointed, at how this was managed. They should only accept smaller groups or have 1 guide per 10 people and keep everyone separated. Yes it was a good experience seeing a turtle try to come out of the sea and another laying eggs but I WOULD NOT recommend going here as it seems to do the turtles more harm than good.
title: Lovely to see, awful experience.

body: This experience brought mixed emotions. It was interesting to see a turtle laying eggs. However we felt Turtle Conservation Project (TCP) were not running it ethically. The group of visitors was too large and the turtle appeared to be stressed. The man running the evening broke many of the rules he outlined in his own briefing to us at the outset, making noise, getting too close etc. We were particularly concerned when the man running the visit started to pull the foliage out around the laying turtle for the group to get a better view, which appeared to stress the turtle further. Running this in a sustainable way, which doesn’t stress the turtles is possible. There should be smaller groups permitted, each with a guide and the guides should not interfere with the turtle as was happening when we visited.
title: Ecotourism gone wrong

body: This was full of around 40 tourists crowding around one turtle. This can’t be good for the turtles! It made me feel really uncomfortable and proof of the downside to tourism. We left the group after 5 minutes. Luckily our driver took us down the beach on our own to see the turtles more peacefully for a little while and without shining any lights but I would not recommend going to the turtle watch.
title: Uncomfortable mass tourism

body: It really was a once in a lifetime chance to see the giant sea turtles laying eggs and going back to the sea, we knew we weren't going to see any hatchlings the night we left but the whole experience was amazing, and as there are no lights it was all under the light of the milky way. Magical. There are some questions about it but I will continue to do my research on how much this bothers the turtles, but they do return yearly to the beaches to lay so I guess not too much. Our group was full of stupid tourists that kept trying to take photos and leaving their flash on, it's a really simple instruction and if you think you can't follow it then don't take your phone out. Nature is more important than your pictures. However, the guides were helpful, it was a very smooth run operation and the 'donation' provides good value for money.
title: Great experience but be thoughtful

body: I have been wanting to see little turtle hatchlings scramble to the ocean for my whole life. It started off well. There wasn't a huge group of tourists and the guide discussed that there were to be no lights, flashes etc, except his red light. I was pleased to hear this. We saw a turtle laying her eggs and he made sure that everyone kept their distance yet so many people either do not listen and use torches, take photos etc, or just don't know how to use them properly and kept setting the flash off by mistake. I don't understand why phones and torches and cameras are just not permitted to be taken with you??? It waas horrible for the poor turtles to be blinded by this and it was incredibly frustrating. The guide did tell people off for it but the group just kept getting bigger and he couldn't control it. By the time we saw the little hatchlings, people were nearly treading on them and flashing their cameras. It would be great if a little trench could be dug by the first guide there, from the nest to the ocean, so that there is no risk of the turtles getting hurt or going the wrong way. If you do go, please respect the rules. These ignorant people really made the situation stressful for those like me who really love the turtles.
title: Best and worst experience - Just take your eyes and leave your camera behind!!!!

body: It a amazing to see a turtle lay her eggs and even hatchlings sprint for the sea. The centre does a great job and tried hard to get people to listen to their instructions- just a shame some people couldn't follow it! Maybe the centre could charge more and limit the numbers to make it a slighter better experience for all.
title: Once in a life time

body: Words cannot explain this. The guide were well informed and gave us all plenty of time to watch the turtle lay her eggs and then cover up before returning to the sea
title: Absolutely amazing. Do not miss this

body: I came to this place tonight and I was told I would see turtles. We were made to wait for 30 minutes in a place there were no turtles and then told to walk another 15 minutes to ‘maybe’ see more turtles. We were led to a bush in the pitch black and told a turtle was inside. I told them after being there for an hour and a half that I wanted a refund. They laughed at me and said ‘no refunds’ and then I was asked to be escorted back in the pitch black along the beach and they didn’t reimburse and I got into an arguement with this cashier and the manager who refused to give me my money back. We almost got into a physical fight because he pushed past me. As a woman this was huge for me and scary. How dare a man rip me off and then physically try to attack me for wanting my money back. BEWARE! SCAM! VIOLENCE and LIES!
title: BEWARE SCAM! NO TURTLES! NO REFUNDS!

body: Ones in a lifetime event. It's nice to see these big turtle grab a huge hole to put their eggs inside. No turtle->no charge
title: Turtle watch

body: Just returned from staying nearby and in 2 minds as to what to think about this. Are we REALLY so desperate to see a poor exhausted turtle or two "doing her thing" to want to stumble along or stand out on a beach (getting bitten by sandflies) for hours in the dark? It WILL be in the dark and lit by infra-red torch light only , making everything rather difficult to see, (and POOR PHOTOGRAPHY if that's what you are there for!). Guides assured us turtles cant hear, just disturbed by white light.Had to assume that our 'fees' would be put to good use and they would take eggs to hatcheries for safety away from tourists. dogs and other preditors.I hadn't realised how much turtle-watching was being promoted as a tourist activity. We certainly felt Sri Lanka needs to be careful where it is going with tourism all round.It has a few safe swimming/surfing beaches (along W/SW stretch at least) and already these look in danger of being swamped and overcrowded very soon. Feared we wouldn't recognise the place in a few years time.
title: Are we so desperate?

body: I was unsure as to whether to go on this tour having read some of the bad reviews.Here's my take:+ magical experience to watch the turtles lay eggs under the moonlight+ guide was very informative and clearly passionate about his conservation work. He was happy to answer all of my questions. - too many selfish tourists who care more about trying to get a selfie with a turtle than its conservation. The guides tried to control the group but many of the tourists failed to follow two simple rules:1. No flash photography 2. Keep your distance.If you do decide to take part in this experience (and it is magical), please follow these simple rules and help the guide to ensure that other tourists follow them too.
title: The tourists (who don't follow the guidelines) are the problem, not the guides

body: No control of numbers, +100 people and one guide with very limited English. Nobody is really protecting the turtles. It’s just a scam to take money from tourists. Try to avoid please.
title: Avoid this experience if you love animals

body: Very well run and controlled by the conservation team. You wait in the information centre until word comes through that a turtle has arrived, it is given time alone before you can approach and under the single red torchlight of the guide you can watch her return to the sea, sometimes without laying any eggs if the sand is not right. Strictly no flash allowed and it can be an exhausting long walk along the soft sand under a pitch black sky... so memorable.
title: What an experience

body: A very hard 2km walk along the beach in the dark – some warning should have been given for just how strenuous this was in soft sand in the dark. The guide went off at a cracking pace and there was no back marker so we soon got left behind. Despite all the initial talk of staying 20m away and only allowing small groups of ten people closer at certain times, in reality it was a free for all with 50 people crowding around a turtle which had just finished laying her eggs. The guide then announced that he would be going to see a second turtle further up the beach which was still laying eggs – at that point we decided to skip the tour and made our way slowly back along the beach. The ideas are fine but the execution is terrible. If you really plan to keep people away and have groups of ten then don’t just have one guide with a group of 50 people – split the tourists into groups of ten at the base, each with a guide and go off in those groups at staggered times.
title: An awful experience

body: Although there was a guide of sorts it was hard to understand what he said and it just seemed a bit indignant for the turtle to be gawked at by a hoard of humans all vying for a look at her laying her eggs. We left the area before the others as it seemed a bit of a freak show. They are making a lot of money from and this hopefully they are getting good advise on the proper procedure...we don’t know enough about turtle protection so maybe they are doing everything correctly? It just didn’t feel right ☹️
title: No organisation felt sorry for the turtle

body: Me and my partner left half way though due to the poor behaviour of tourists and this being more like a photography shoot of the Turtles that we did not want to be a part of. This was very badly managed for people claiming to ‘protect the turtles’ and unless the way this is managed changes I would not recommend anyone to go! Despite the guide stating no flashes and being 20m away from the Turtle about 40 people were running towards the turtles far too close and at least 15 peoples flashes went off (which blinds them) we spent most of our time feeling sorry for the turtle and angry at other tourists behaviour rather than enjoying any of the experience which is why we decided to leave. It was unable to be managed properly by the guide due to the number of tourists trying to get to this poor turtle. My advise to this conservation project is put the turtles first not the money! run this in small groups of approx 6-8 people max where distance from the turtle and phones can be managed better! Do this and people might be even willing to pay a bit more (we certainly would have been) Running in small groups means1.you get a more personal experience 2.the project is run in the best interest of the turtles not tourists 3.people will pay more to avoid crowds 4. Also some more information about what the money contributes towards in regards to helping you guys manage this project ( I am sure you do a great job but we didn’t know exactly what you did or how the money paid contributed). I really hope you make some changes on how this is run and the turtles and people visiting will be much happier!
title: Badly managed! Change is needed!

body: 58 people surrounding one poor endangered green turtle as she desperately tried to lay her eggs. We were told no flash for photography, only we listened. The mostly chinese tourists did not care for her wellbeing and took selfies with her, shouting and laughing. I was crying in anger and trying to tell people to get back, be quiet and stop littering as the tour guide laughed at me and occasionally asked people to step back.Beach dogs roamed freely, I love dogs but they dig up turtle nests - the nest should be guarded or protected... and not with more plastic to litter the oceans with! Where is the money going from the tourists?? Certainly not to education and turtle welfare!!! Disgusted with myself for taking part. Sri Lanka. Be ashamed.
title: Disgusting abuse

body: When high season, the event is far overcrowded and somehow humíiating for the happening itself.. Much better in April, when there are only a few visitors..And dont forget snack! It takes hours..Anyway to see it is really special.. just be ready to ignore the turism around..Kids were happy to see it, so we are
title: Better than nothing..

body: This is an amazing chance to see large turtles coming on shore to dig their nest, lay eggs, cover them and retreat back to sea. We got to see two turtles do exactly that. It was a 10 minute walk for us on the night. Its all nature dependant in regards to duration and walking distance. The guides are there to guide you only. Research turtles yourself before you go. We had a very annoying person shouting at the guides to be quiet on our trip and complaining it was taking too long!!!Turtles cannot hear human voices! Please educate yourself before going. Also please remember no flash! Three people did this on our watch, its just embarrassing. The guides were friendly and the cost ($5) is incredible. Other countries you would pay hundreds of dollars. Don't be an embarrassing tourist and you will have an amazing experience.
title: Turtle power

body: Its totally reassuring that these people give the priority to the Turtles first and thats how it should be. After visiting Rekewa beach and speaking to Saman who has 20+ years experience you then realize that hes not after the tourists money. Even then, they will only take a small fee of about £5 if a turtle turns up on the beach. He says that baby turtles only have 3 days energy from their yoke sack to get them out into deep water. Whereas at Hasselblad further along the coast they keep babies in a concrete tank to swim around for 3 days using up vital energy before they release them? Nice for tourists to see but not good for the turtles? At Rekewa beach they only dig up the eggs if they are too close to the sea because sea water would kill the eggs, even then they do that within 6 hours and only move them to a safer position. Plus they patrol the beach 24 hours a day. This is conservation at its best. We were only there for around 10 minutes before we got the call that there was a Olive Ridley Turtle and a large Green Turtle on the beach laying eggs. They dont allow any white light because it will disturb the turtle. It was a magical experience watching how hard the Turtles worked to dig the holes, lay the eggs and then struggle to get back to the sea. They do allow you to take photos and film but flashes are a No No. The red light that the guides use are sufficient for good footage. A truly Magical experience. Hats off to them for their passion and commitment.
title: Turtles come first!

body: Be prepared for a long night and a fairly long walk along the beach. It IS WORTH IT. We were so lucky to see not 1 but 3 turtles. It would be very useful if you took a torch that has a red filter on it as this is what is needed to watch the Turtles without disturbing them. If you have a torch that you don't need it would be great if you could take it and leave it with them as getting good quality torches in Sri Lanka seems difficult.The staff are all very knowledgeable and take care that visitors do not disturb the Turtles. Seeing Turtles isn't guaranteed, I hope that you are as lucky as we were
title: We saw 3 Turtles!!!

body: Spent 4 days as a family assisting this project - beach patrol in evenings looking for turtles, beach clean-up and nest checking during day and helping with visitors. To be clear this is a community project with a 24 hour roster, set up to encourage community responsibility for the nesting turtles (instead of egg and shell poaching)We saw turtles every night (3 on one night), if none arrive nobody is charged. Money goes towards paying local people for beach patrols and nest protection. Controlling a large group of tourists is difficult when some just turn up from hotels and are not given to orientation talk and through language difficulty - guides do the best they can, pushy tourists cause the scrum around the turtles.. Information about turtles and the project is available but in our experience rarely read by visitors. Facilities do need to be refreshed.
title: Local Conversation Effort

body: I have been to beaches where turtles nest. This beach is about "one turtle" and that's all you will see. At moment it felt as if the turtle was put there by someone for the show to begin and make some money out of a beautiful helpless creature and curious tourists. I have had a really nice time in Sri Lanka but people need to watch out for things like this. It may be a scam but I might be wrong. You are made to wait an hour. The turtle suddenly arrives. Its interesting to point out that the guide says "the turtle" not "a turtle". 45 people are then amassed on to a single turtle ( that's 45,000 rupees or around €300 ). The poor turtle then hurries away towards the sea clearly stressed out. Something simply doesn't feel right at this right. I regret having gone
title: I think it's a scam

body: Horrible place, don't go there. It's a scam. They ask Rp 1000 for entrance. I doubt that there is any money spent on the wellbeing of the turtles. The group we had was way too big (40 people). They steal money of old people who can not walk so good. We had a long walk on the beach in the sand and one of us had a handicap and they tried to "help", very roughly and pushing and pulling and after several requests to stop with that he did not. He followed us till we were back in the tuk tuk and asked money. It was a shame and we didn't give one Rupee. During the turtle watch the guide did not tell us anything about the turtles. I am sure if there were more tourists to watch the turtles they would explore that and the maximum of 10 people is a lie. It a business of moneymaking on helpless creatures.
title: Horrible

body: You turn up to a building with National Geographic showing on TV. A lion killing a wilderbeast. There are some very worn out pictures and dusty charts about turtles. The idea is that you hang around until a turtle comes ashore to lay eggs. Once she starts the guilded tour brings with the tourists led to the beach to watch. When we visited around 50 people were waiting. These slowly left and we left at 10pm. No sign of turtle, no charge. Not sure how good for nesting turtles this would be. Avoid
title: Waste of time and money. No conservation evidence

body: To stop poaching thr turtles' Eggs is worth every effort. So please go thete to suppose those guys. If they would not be thete all turtles would have been extinct ever since.. clear recommenation !
title: Good to help protect the turtles

body: Being from the east coast of the United States, I thought I knew a lot about the sea turtles but I learned a lot! They work very hard to save hurt and handicapped sea turtles. In addition, they have a hatchery and protect them before releasing them at an age where they have a larger chance of survival. It was very interesting but they need donations!
title: Totally worth a visit!

body: Only a small cost but a very worthwhile experienceVery knowledgable and informative guide who involved everyoneAs well as treating injured turtles and where possible returning them to the sea, they receive eggs from people and they hatch them with an over 70 percent success rate, and return them to the sea
title: Amazing well worth a visit

body: This place is a good start to tell people about the turtel problem; they need to be saved as fast es possible!!!Tonight there were over 40 People and it was pland to go with all to the beach hold a distance from 20 meter and go with "small" groups from 10 People closer to the turtel, up to 1meter, that is absolutly to much!!! Good would be to make a limit by 20 People and to go in small groops with 3 people + guide to the turtle; so the guide had more control about the stupid tourists. Then it would be a much better place.I have not liked the idea of stressing the turtle and i was driving home without seeing the beach. At the beginning one guide was explaning about turtel in a very bad english maybe it is possible to find some passionated volunteers to do this with a better English as well it could be a tourist only for 2 nights and then the next one.This could be a very good way to spread importend informations. Pleas read about "4 Ocean" they have in January a special turtel project
title: Stressed turtels

body: I’m writing to raise some concerns about this turtle watch tour running at Rekawa Beach, Sri Lanka (on the south coast). We have never joined tours as such and did not know what to expect. I didn’t realise they were the endangered green turtles that I would be seeing. The tours run from 8:30pm till late, during the season when green sea turtles come to be beach to lay eggs. We join the tour in early January 2019. It charges 10,000 Sri Lankan Rupees per person. The tour we joined we had about 40 people in one group. There were about 3 staff members leading us to where the green turtle digs the egg chambers. Only red lights were allowed on the beach, no flash allowed. My concerns with the tour and the staff are as follows:- it was a rather big group and most refused to listen to the volunteers to stand further away from the turtle while they wait for their turn- we were awfully close to the green turtle while she was laying her eggs, like we were literally just an arm-length away from the turtle and her eggs.- the staff was shouting on the beach to direct tourists- the Rekawa Beach does not have restricted access, only paid entry between 7pm-6am- we saw one big fishing nets on the beach (during day time)My husband and I left the group early, we only saw the turtle laying eggs and as she was burying the eggs, we didn’t know how long the group stayed and what they saw after. We felt awful about disturbing the turtles. I’m not sure where and whom to write to, and wondering if this tour group requires some sort of monitoring / staff training to run these tour groups, if allowed at all. I felt that the operation of the nightly tour groups is causing major levels of disturbance. Of course there are also a few people who did not turn their flash off as they take pictures.I hope this message will be forwarded to the relevant conversation organisation for consideration.
title: Rekawa beach and tour operation require stricter monitoring

body: The guides were excellent and provide lots of great information about the area and the turtles. We saw turtles nesting and hatching. Great night.
title: Awesome experience.

body: A must do, if waiting on a beach is too much for you, try this. Disabled friendly, interesting and turtles close up.
title: Fantastic experience

body: It was well organized and they made sure that none of us uses the mobile flash and everyone gets a chance to see the Turtle laying eggs in night without disturbing the creature
title: Informative

body: We just lived next door in the green turtle hotel (which we can recommend!) and went there. We saw the turtles (2) putting their eggs down in a hole at the beach, which was amazing and we were really lucky to see that! We would have loved getting more informations because you can just read something before the small walk to the beachs starts but this is it. However, great experience and worth seeing it. (On the 2nd oic you see the back of the turtle from very close with its tail and an egg coming out–the white thing).
title: We saq the turtles!

body: It's an informative evening that directly helps the conservation of turtles. At nightfall everyone gathers at the ticket office where we were told what to do and what to expect. We followed our ranger when he received information that some turtles had come ashore. We followed him with a red flashlight for about 500 meters. Ounce the turtle starts laying her eggs we were aloud to get close enough to watch. After the eggs are laid the turtle buries the eggs and returns to the sea. Great evening. So worth it.
title: Evening to remember

body: While staying in the area, I heard about this place and had my doubts about visiting in case it was an organization that cared more about money than turtles (common in SL). After reading many reviews i decided to give it a shot, and fortunately it looked to me like their programme is genuine. I didn’t feel in any moment that turtles were harrased or misstreated to make the tourist happier, which is what I cared about the most. Briefly, after a turtle was spotted, we were asked to pay the 1000 rupees (they dont get your money if no turtle is seen) and we set off to a beach 5 min away. We had to wait (45 min) as the turtle was digging the nest hole (cant be disturbed then). While laying eggs, the turtle could be observed in reduced groups and from a fair distance, using only red light (cant be seen by the turtle). My personal experience was amazing since all the tourists got tired after a while and i had the pleasure to stay on my own with the two guides till the end. After laying the eggs, the turtle covers the hole (more than 1 hour) and finally heads towards the sea. I would recommend this for two main reasons: 1) it’s a wonderful experience; 2) i believe your money positively contributes to preserve turtle breeding in that area. Guides well very communicative, with good English and knowledge of turtle behaviour.
title: Better than expected! Recommended!

body: We were there at 8pm & had to wait an hour or so & word came there was a turtle on the beach, we set off after another hour & reached the turtle after 20 minutes walking.It was great to see her making a nest from a distance then up really close when she was laying her eggs.The guide was great & very helpful answering any questions. Allow at least 4 hours to see this from start to finish, it's really worth it.
title: Turtle Watching

body: We save the turtle and our planet by helping those who are already doing so. wonderful turtle show, not to be missed
title: We save the turtles

body: We were staying in accommodation right next to the tour area, so decided that we would join the tour for the experience. We understand that the tour guides are volunteers but their initial explanation of what was going to happen was very poor and they just seemed to be rattling off information as quick as they could before taking us down to the sand.No explanation was given as to what to expect and we stayed on the beach waiting for something! When we asked the only information was that we were waiting!Eventually we saw a turtle heading back to the water, not sure if she had laid eggs or not. Then we walked back in the dark - no further explanations.The next day we walked along the beach area where we had been in the dark and were disgusted to see the piles of rubbish in the turtle watching area - an area that is meant to be under wild life protection. Not something that I would do again. Too many people, not enough information and not sure that all the money paid heads in the right direction.
title: Wouldn't do this again

body: It was really worth it. The guide answers all our doubts. We only go near the turtle when they are sure the turtle is safe. We saw 3 turtles.
title: Worth it

body: A magical visit with the Turtle Watch volunteers. Spending a few hours on the beach with them waiting for turtles then watching them lay their eggs was a once-in-a-lifetime experience. The visit is well organised and at the volunteers ensure that the turtles are not disturbed and that visitors can only approach a nesting turtle at the appropriate moment. Such dedication - the volunteers do this every single night. A presentation about Sri Lanka's turtles precedes the beach visit. Then you sit and wait, hoping that the call arrives to say a turtle has arrived on the beach.
title: A green turtle at midnight

body: An amazing experience to watch a turtle laying her eggs and covering them before eh aiding back to sea. We arrive about 8:30 and I think we left around 11 or 11:30. Initially we all sat waiting on the beach for a long time, I think waiting for the turtles to make their pit, but they didn’t really let us know. There were a lot of people, but they split us into two groups to watch two different turtles. They tried to enforce only 10 people watching at a time but people weren’t really listening which was a shame. Perhaps they should cap how many people they allow per night. They didn’t talk too much, but we’re happy to answer questions when asked.
title: Worth the wait

body: We visited this place with our kids aged 8, 10 and 12. The entrance fee is 500 rupies per person but our little one didn’t have to pay. A guide explained to us the different species of turtles in Sri Lanka. He then showed us the dozen or so injured turtles they saved with the help of fishermen and that they are trying to rehabilitate and return to the ocean. We also saw two months old and three days old babies. The kids could hold some of the turtles. It was a nice and interesting stop on our way to Galle. We all loved it!
title: Very interesting and we can hold the turtles

body: Appreciate that this is a way to make money by locals and also to help conservation but the way the tour is run is very poor. No explanation of what is going on. Too many people talking loudly, pushing and running to try and get to the poor turtle first with no concern for its welfare. I felt saddened to be part of the experience. If you are an animal lover this may upset you.
title: Too many people

body: Reviews for this place are very Marmite, but for us is was a good experience. Perhaps because we stayed very close to the Turtle Watch, so we perhaps were given the inside track. We had not planned to go Turtle Watching as we had read it was out of season, we were just there for a place to stay after visiting the brilliant Karamatiya Eco Bird Watching that afternoon / evening. We visited a simple local restaurant who looked after us well and told us when a turtle had been spotted by the "spotters". Only then were we taken by Tuk Tuk to buy our tickets and then to the place on the beach near to where the turtle had been found. We saw the laying, the burying and the going back out to sea (through the rough surf). There were perhaps 20 people, no use of flash, only red light, and little noise, and kept to the rear and side of her, so limited stress for the turtle. One person was supervising the people and another was supervising the laying. This second person was very happy to answer questions quietly, and was very informative. All this on a moonlit beach with pounding surf, worth £20 of anybody's money for our family of 4.
title: Had a good experience, and the turtle seemed to also

body: We were fortunate enough to see a turtle lay her eggs and bury them. Pretty cool thing to witness. We were impressed that the guides very contius of not disturbing the turtles in any way.
title: Giant turtle

body: This is an organisation focussed on $. We were there with our kids of 12 and 15 and with another 100 people. When one of the turtles was stuck in the roots of a plant while laying eggs, two men of the organisation started digging and pulling the turtle loose. This is not a natural way and the stress for these animals was huge. We saw only one turtle covered by sand, that was it. Also kids seem to be last in line while some people who paid some extra could go first.... bad experience! People who were late came first too... not organised at all.
title: Terrible...

body: Visit when you are around the area. One of the best place to see turtles from the wild. Partly Supported by Ocean Park in Hong Kong, Definately worth visiting at night 8:30pm or early morning.
title: Best place to see sea turtles

body: 1000 rupees for NOTHING. No organization, information, nothing. Horrible experience, a classical tourist trap. Poor turtle chased by the group of ppl.
title: What a disaster

body: Was unsure when we stopped here as I really wanted this to have a sincere conservation focus. Generally it was interesting and informative. The staff handled the turtles quite a lot which made me uncomfortable but their efforts did seem genuine and overall it was apparent to me this was a positive project.

we went there in June during hatching season and could watch some huge water turtles lay eggs for one hour. the guides were very concerned about the animals, told us how to behave, forbid light and we weren't allowed to touch any turtles or get in their way.we had to speak very quietly and not move too close or too fast.this is a really nice projec,t which also keeps the beaches clean and protects the animals.
title: nice project, real animal protection, trustworthy guides

body: Visited with a small group and had the opportunity to follow a green turtle laying eggs as well as returning to the ocean. Took 3 hours and was mesmerising! Recommended for fellow turtle lovers
title: Good project

body: We went during low season and given previous reviews, we were cynical. Our experience however was really good, we (the group) had an excellent guide (we went on Monday 30th), he showed us videos of turtles hatching, and helped us understand the process. While out on the beach, he focused on 1 green turtle who was laying eggs, and returned to the sea. Some people left as soon as they had seen her laying, it was definitely worth watching the whole process though, her return back to the sea was beautiful if not a little long :) Definitely worth the visit. This is nature, sometimes you’re lucky and you see something and sometimes you don’t. The guys at the conservation project were making the utmost effort to keep people entertained and to answer questions. The beach is also stunning at night and it was lovely hearing the waves and the wildlife.
title: Worth a visit!!

body: We were keen to support this local initiative, which is advertised as sensitive to the turtle’s needs. Duly wore dark clothing, left our phones and cameras in the hotel and paid our 1000 rupees each. So disappointed to arrive at the turtle nesting site with dozens of other people, many of whom were talking and using flash photography. The poor turtle trying to lay her eggs was distracted and then moved off without completing her laying. As the crowd prepared to follow, we decided enough was enough and headed back to our hotel £20 poorer and sad to have contributed to the turtle’s distress. Wish I had checked the reviews first!
title: Avoid if you care about turtle wellbeing

body: I must have been on the same night as Dede and James.Its not very well organised and there are too many people all trying to get the best view of a tired big sea turtle who just wants to be left alone.It would have been much better to limit access in smaller groups but that snot how it worked on the night.My son struggled to get a view because no one would move away from a good viewing location.Having said this we did see a sea turtle on the beach which isn't an everyday thing for us. However this amazing experience was spoiled by the other free for all from the other people, we just left after seeing the turtle because the other people were so annoying.Staff need to enforce tighter control and limit the numbers who can go near the turtles, split the group into 8-10 people at a time and let everyone get a good view not just the forceful few.
title: Saw a Turtle Just!

body: BE AWARE The people working at the conservation project centre have been doing this for more than 20 years, they accept tourists to visit because it pays the bills and they also donate this money to the village of Rekawa so people won't resort to poaching and steal the eggs for money.That said. The only problem with this tours aren't the way it's organised or handled. The BIG issue here are the tourists. We all know, when people pay to see something, they wanna see it now, they wanna touch it, they wanna be in the first row, taking photos, living the experience. We understand, that's how humans are. Although this made the experience less than it should have been. I blame the tourists who (even after being told thousands upon thousands of times) still used the flash on their cameras. We were about 30 people surrounding a poor turtle lying eggs and people were pushing each other and throwing their kids at the turtle. People need to chill. If you wanna live this experience, RESPECT the animal yourself. The guides do their best to handle a bunch or crazy tourists who won't even listen to their CLEAR guidelines.This is out of the way.We weren't sure at first when the tour started because the amount of people was overwhelming. Although at the very end, most the of the tourists left (around 12am) we had the chance of staying at a small villa near the beach so we didn't have to catch a tuktuk or bus back in town. We took our time, and good thing we did. We were 8 tourists left on the beach and we happened to see hatchlings go back to the see. We had a chat with our guide about the conservation project, their goals, what they do to help, etc.All this to say. Don't be one of those tourists who ruin the whole experience for everyone. Take the time to listen and watch the turtles in respect.
title: People need to miss the point. IMPORTANT INFORMATION!!!!!

body: i disagree that the conservation causes more harm than good. they tidy the beach and prevent active poaching. however, it was shocking to watch little babyturtles being «guided» to the sea by some complete fool of a tourist who litterally tried to take matters into his own hands. he was sort of picking up a baby turtle and tossing it in the right direction and using white light. we managed to stop him, but the guides should provide better info, and they should spend more donation on rule enforcement other than the people, this was the most amazing expierence
title: fantastic experience, terribly organized

body: After doing some research into turtle watching I was not convinced we'd find somewhere that managed tourism properly, and sadly this place did not exceed expectations. We were informed by our guest house that it was a project aimed at protecting turtles and would be the best thing we did in sri lanka. while there is no doubt that this project has been effective in stopping the area getting built up and therefore has done some good conservation work, the experience overall was not a pleasant one.we were in a group of around 30 people and were very clearly told not to use lights of any kind as it is traumatic for the turtles, yet there were 5 separate occasions where tourists disregarded this rule either in order to use their phone or take a flash photo. while the guides did remind tourists of the rules, they were not able to enforce them. we got way too close to the turtles, and even when it was just the guides using red light, the turtles definitely knew we were there and seemed to make a dash for the sea. we were clearly disrupting their nesting.until tighter rules are enforced (such as making tourists out their phones in lockers before heading out, having a max group size of 10, and staying at least 5 meters away from the nesting turtles at all times), i would not recommend this trip. we came away feeling very guilty
title: Such a shame

body: The Turtle Watch was on our „must do list“ for Sri Lanka. We saw one turtle on its way back to the sea and to be honest I wasn’t aware how big they are. The guide was a good one. He always was taking care that tourists don’t step too close to the turtle. Unfortunately no moon light and flashing is forbidden what is logical. So taking good pictures was a challange... To satisfy people interested in watching more turtles the guide offered another location. Overall a great experience and worth to do it and support in parallel the protection of these animals.
title: Great Experience

body: We were very lucky to see big green turtle preparing the room for the eggs.She had more then 100 eggs!The guide has red lights, it is possible filming and making photos without flash.Actually the red light is perfect for the camera.It is very romantic experience!In order to see the turtles and do not loose too much time in waiting, we get the hotel 30 m from the beach.The hotel is in constant contact with guides, so we were called at the right time!Thank you!Laviniq
title: So romantic and natural place

body: Last night we were lucky enough to watch a green turtle nesting on the beach.. We only had a short wait before we were informed she had arrived. Although the group was quite large the visitors were for the most part quiet and respectful. We stayed about 20m away while she dug her nesting hole and were then taken in small groups to view her laying the eggs. The turtle was not disturbed by this. Once she had finished laying all her eggs we watched her cover the hole.Many visitors left at this point. We were extremely lucky to then see some hatchlings make their way to the sea. It was beautiful to watch.After a while we also watched mum come out of the nest and make her way back into the sea. It was a magical and humbling experience and we were so lucky to have witnessed it.I would strongly recommed this experience.
title: Fantastic turtle watch

body: i went to this place last month.i sow one big turtle came to baech and laying their eggs..i never seen this activity before,as well as thank you for all the people who work in this project..
title: Nice place to watch sea turtle

body: On a whim we wanted to find some turtles. Our Tuk Tuk driver took us to the Turtle Conservation Project to join the other tourists also wanting to find some turtles. It's very casual. Generally you should arrive around 8:00pm - 8:30pm - this is apparently the best time to catch a sight of turtles laying eggs on the beach or coming up to the beach or going back to the ocean. There were about 20 people who wanted to do this as well. We were given a good brief by the volunteers and workers that do this job 24 hours/day. The conservation museum is worth going to learn about the turtle facts and how conservation is important. You are not allowed flash photography of course, it's pretty dark when you go down to the beach and the only real light is coming from the full moon - which is amazing. When we went down, a green turtle had already come up to the beach and she was laying her eggs. You need to stay at least 20 meters away and you approach turtles from the back. We stayed for about 20 minutes when we realized that in order to see her, we would need to wait another 60-90 minutes. It takes 45 minutes for her to lay her eggs and another 45 minutes for her to cover them with sand and then she will traverse back to the ocean. We didn't have that kind of time so we left but with more patience I'm sure we would have seen her and been really stoked about it. Lots of kids and parents, families, couples - it's a cool experience but make sure you have time.
title: Cool if you have time

body: This should have been one of those special moments in your life but it wasn't owing to the size of the party allowed to observe - we were in a group of 50 that was split into 3 sub groups when viewing the turtle. Yes it was great to see a turtle through the whole process; laying its eggs was amazing and watching it return to the sea was beautiful. But like other reviews, we were far from convinced that this viewing from such a large party was in the interest of the turtle. We went to Uganda last year where viewing of chimps and gorillas were each restricted to groups of 8. So how come 50+ works for turtles and when laying their eggs?!
title: The cumulative average score from all previous reviews says it all

body: Unfortunately, this experience wasn't what we hoped it would be.The 'experience' involves hundreds of tourists crowding over one poor turtle trying to lay their eggs. There is no organisation - just people rushing to get into the groups to surround the turtle who has a red light flashed onto it for over an hour and hundreds of people, gawking, pointing and moving in front of it. Apparently it's fine to use a red light and your not allowed to use a normal light or flash but the red light looks pretty disturbing to me! Despite being told not to use a flash camera, many prople "accidentally" used flash to get a good photo of the turtle, resulting in the distressed animal pausing its laying for periods after each flash. The 'conservationists' seemed more interested in the tourist experience than the turtle, loudly shouting "next group forward"...this can hardly be soothing for the turtle either.We were told that the turtle was knackered because she had tried to lay her eggs last night, but was disturbed, so was having another go tonight. 1) I'm sure the disturbance was probably last nights 200+ guests.2) surely tonight was then a night to leave the poor thing alone and not subject her to another 200 people.We weren't quite sure what the 1,000 rupees per person 'conservation' is for? It's a funny way of protecting the species, by disturbing them laying eggs. Surely a better way would be to leave them alone? We have been to other Turtle laying sites such as Lankayan Island in Borneo. There only guests can watch the turtles (meaning a max of 30 people at a time, hid well out of site). This surely is a much better way of protecting and conserving the species than the carnage in Sri Lanka.
title: Not a very humane way to watch turtles!

body: We went there without knowing what to expect - the experience could not have been worse. First, you meet at a little cottage where you get an explanation on turtels in general and how to behave during the guided tour. We were already negativly surprised about the 150 to 200 people there. Second, we were all guided as one (!) group to the beach where we waited until one turtle was spotted. So far - so good. The horrible experience started when groups of 30 persons and more were guided to the turtle. The poor animal was surrounded by shouting and flashing tourists. None of the before mentioned rules was respected nor enforced. Our conclusion: A total fail! Invest those 1.000 Rupies in another project in case you care for animals.
title: Horrible experience!

body: This village community project is second to none. The guides and conservationist top notch and professional. We went during a full moon and were so fortunate. We saw a baby turtle hatch and go into the sea, four huge turtles laying eggs and digging holes and two adult turtles going back I to the surf once in a lifetime. We stayed at Beach Villa Rekawa à stand alone house on the beach great location and the staff were amazing.
title: Once in a lifetime

body: we saw 2 enormous big turtles digging their holes, laying their eggs and walking back to the ocean. it's a spectacle, we really enjoyed the experience. furthermore the sky was so clear and during the waiting times we were busy with starwatching. the turtle conservation project should be supported, they do a really great job.
title: amazing experience at turtle watch

body: I suspected it would be the case, but they allow so many people on the beach at the same time that's it chaos and no one listens to the don't run or get to close instructions. Better than local fisherman eating turtle eggs. Which I've seen. So it's a step in the right direction. But perhaps a limit to the number of tourists and a first come first serve basis? The staff were great though, working hard.
title: Too many tourists! Which I was one of

body: I felt as though the guides acted with respect for the turtles here. They really appear to care that their actions do not disturb the natural behaviour of the animals and put this before the wants of tourists which was important to me. I’d recommend the experience but be warned it’s a very popular attraction.
title: Great experience

body: I know it’s run by volunteers so it’s a bit disingenuous to criticise too much, but there was more wrong with the trip than right. The group was far too big and poorly supervised. There wasn’t enough information as to precisely what would happen ( and how long it would take) and, because the group was too big, people were getting too close to the turtles and using camera phones to try and take pictures which should have been a strict no-no. At least one turtle did not lay eggs for whatever, maybe because of us or maybe not. Having seen several of the massive and beautiful creatures, it felt good at the time, but looking back, I wonder if, even with our donations to protect the turtles, we did more harm than good.
title: Should have been better
