body: They were very adamant about the fact that people should keep lights and phones turned off. Only red light to be used in order not to disturb the turtles. Done in a very respectful manner.
title: Respect for the turtles

body: I would say. Dont go. Maybe it is well meant but the setup is completely wrong. They claim to protect the turtles nests financed by the entrancefees of the tourists which is fine but the groups are way to big. People are not supposed to use their flash on their cameras or phones but amongst the group of 50+ people there are too many tourists who are too ignorant or not able to understand their mobile phones. Its a disgrace!The one guide is not able to keep control over it and even dissapeared for at least 10 minutes leaving those tourists breaking all the rules. A family was shooting family portrets with their flashes after they had seen the turtles!, there by scaring other turtles in the ocean away and probably disturbed the nesting turtle . It was one of the saddest thing i have seen in Sri Lanka and definetely doesnt make you feel better if you have a heart for animals. Even if you will not break any of the rules which comes with watching turtles, this is not exactly how you want to feel after watching one of this beautyful animals giving birth.
title: Groups too big, scaring the turtles while giving birth

body: It's a miracle of ages - to see the turtle nesting. If you are nearby - it's a must attend. Usually they gather people at 8 pm, but even if you'll come at 10 pm - you will not loose anything important.
title: Touch of nature

body: Visitors pay the poachers to convince them not to damage the turtles nests. They call it donation. Apart from that the visit is quite tiring - 2-3 hours at night and few kilometers walk on the beach. Before that at least 1 hr waiting (but this time is efficiently used for collecting the obligatory donations).
title: Commercial project, not for animals

body: This is definitely a must do if you are in Tangalle! Saw a sea turtle lady eggs and then go back to the oven. The guide explained everything quite well and was also concerned for the turtles as he would only take about 10 persons at a time and did not allow bright lights and flash photos as these would disturb and scare the turtle. One person was actually told off for looking at his phone, which was emitting bright light. The size of the turtle amazed us and also the effort it she was putting in to cover the eggs properly. She was so tired afterwards that she had to stop a few times on her way back to the ocean.
title: Amazing experience

body: Reached this area around 9pm and was turned away. Guards stated that the area was closed because turtles have been spotted and then left so none were expected. The whole place seemed poorly organised and lacking in proper administration. Disappointed as this was supposed to be one of the highlights of the area.
title: Disappointed

body: There were tons of people at first and it made it really hard to enjoy being there and even harder to glimpse any turtles. After quite a while the crowd started to disperse and then it got a lot better. We were able to see several turtles digging and laying, and even got to help one who got stuck! It was pretty lousy at first, but the end made it worth it.
title: It was okay

body: We deliberately booked a guest house in Ranna to coincide with Poya and full moon to see turtles and support conservation. Then read the reviews on trip advisor and spoke with our local guest house. If the crowds were too distressing for visiting families, can you imagine how it is for an exhausted turtle? So try this as an experience.....go visit the conservation project during the day, there are knowledgable people there and you can walk the beach and see the sand trails from both adult turtles and hatchlings. You can walk in their foot steps without disturbing them and know you are in their nesting areas, without intimidating them, and you don't join the melee at night and don't contribute to the disturbances. Ok so you don't have a photo of you in front of a turtle but are you going there for your benefit or to support turtle conservation???????????? Please, think about the impact of hundreds of tourists on these dependent animals and behave responsibly. Do support the conservation work but can some of you, all of you do it selflessly ?
title: Try something different....FOR THE SAKE OF THE TURTLES

body: We were staying at the Green Turtle guest house right next to the so-called conservation site and decided we’d like to go for a walk on the beach around 10.00pm. We did not know about the ‘tours’ that are organised. After walking down to the beach we were immediately surrounded by 3 locals, apparently because they had t-shirts with turtle badges on this made them ‘official turtle conservationists’. We were told we couldn’t walk on the beach unless we paid LKR1000 as a ‘donation’. We politely refused this donation and tried to walk away along the public beach but we were shouted at and immediately set upon and ordered off of the beach. Their attitude was extremely aggressive especially in front of women and children. I cannot believe we were held to ransom in the name of turtle conservation. Avoid this tourist scam at all costs!!!!
title: Aggressive attitudes towards women in front of children.... Avoid this rip off in the name of conservation!

body: I can't confirm the negative ratings. Yes, there were quite a few people - but that is hardly the fault of the project. They managed it quite well, ensuring that everybody gets to see the turtle for a few minutes while the others had to stand back.As they should, they were very strict about only using red light (no flash) and not standing in front of the turtle. They also only allowed anyone close once she had finished digging the egg chamber and started laying, when the chances of disturbance are minimal.As regards disturbing her with noise, everyone around was quiet and even walked softly. Yes, of course the guide spoke loudly, but human speech is not in their hearing range, or at least the sensitive part of it - evidence suggests that they hear low frequency sounds and otherwise react to vibrations and air displacement.I really wish people informed themselves a bit before trashing a community-led conservation initiative. Far from not giving benefits to turtles, the fact that now the community can earn money by protecting the nests has made a world of difference. Yes, it means one or two turtles per night have to put up with being watched while laying eggs, but it has saved thousands of clutches since the project was started in the 90s. So please go, don't begrudge them the 1000 rupees and follow the instructions, and it will not harm the turtles and provide income to many families at the same time.
title: Worth a visit for wildlife lovers!

body: Nice, but few turtles. Waited too long as people kept arriving, and the turtle had already ended its pounding.
title: Turtle watch

body: A great evening, spotting turtles on the beach, we were lucky and got to see an Olive Ridley laying its eggs
title: Turtles

body: Firstly, you may not see a turtle. The team patrol the beaches 24/7 to protect the nesting sites, but they can't guarantee a sighting. We were lucky, we waited until about 9.30 and then a green turtle was spotted nesting. Before this, we were given a talk on turtles in Sri Lanka, and the threats they face, which is why protected beaches are so very important. Some people came very late and missed the talk, but the leader gave it again. He also answered questions. We were briefed very clearly about how to approach turtles, and how we would not approach until the turtle was settled, and how we would need to be quiet and not use flash and torches, only the red lights provided. Of course, some people did use flash occasionally, which I think was an accident but was really disappointing. However, they did get told off.I was concerned about how many of us were crowding round the turtle, but they team kept us back whilst also moving us around so we could all see. We were there a few hours. I thought it would disturb the turtle, but it did not seem to - she nested, laid her eggs and very slowly crawled back to the sea. It was amazing to watch. The team care very much about conservation in Sri Lanka and want people to understand how amazing the turtles are, and other wildlife. They need and deserve more help and funding than they currently get. I would recommend people go to this, stay back and behave themselves, and donate to turtle conservation!
title: Worth supporting - dedicated staff but they need more funding and support from local government.

body: We saw 3 green turtles, two were in the process of covering their eggs when we got there and the other was heading back to the sea after a false crawl (where they bottle it half way through).It was amazing to witness the effort it takes for these creatures to lay their eggs but I think a few simple things could have made it better.At the start there were probably over 100 people heading to the beach. These were being shepherded by one man with limited English. No matter how good he was at controlling the crowd, and he did ok, there needed to be more staff as some of the crowd were blatantly ignoring instructions.Once we saw the first turtle a lot of people left (mainly the ones that weren’t listening to the guide) so it was a lot nicer watching the next one. I recommend staying longer and letting the crowd die down. At this time of year, you are likely to see more than one turtle anyway.Finally, although the displays were informative, they could have been more up to date with an emphasis on where our 1000 rupees was being spent - as they are certainly making some money! There was very little information on what the organisation did apart from arrange tours to see the turtles. Overall it was an amazing (5*) experience to see the turtles but they need more staff to manage the number of people that go every night, and they need to be clearer on what conservation work they do.
title: Great experience but could be better organised

body: There are mixed reviews as to the experience with turtles once they land. I can't comment on how the experience pans out once a turtle lands on the beach as we didn't see any turtles. However what you may well do is wait. Now maybe you'll be lucky like some reviewers and have a turtle already there or arriving soon after you arrive.But you'd need to be very lucky at the moment if the tally of turtles recently observed is representative of the current level of activity.One turtle was observed on each of the two nights before we attended.we arrived at around 8.15 and left at a little past 11 pm with not one word of any arrival.50 people must have left before us and very few remained.To be fair they did not charge in advance and of course there are no promises made.These are after all wild creatures.Anyway I'd say some conservation is better than none and I have no reason to doubt the bonafides of this organisation but don't go thinking you will necessarily see turtles. You may well not.i can only rate our experience and it was not a highlight!Mike Melb,Australia
title: As long as you understand what you are signing up for

body: We arrived expecting to walk on the beach and see turtles beside a small amount of tourists - this was not the case. Instead we arrived via tuk tuk and paid 2000 rupees, where 150 people were being spoken to by 1 guide who was wearing a silly hat, obviously killing the time whilst waiting for the signal from the man on the beach keeping a close eye on where the turtle was heading to lay eggs. After sinking 1 beer and smoking 6 fags we were eventually allowed to go on the beach. At first the thought of seeing a turtle was exciting but soon that fire was extinguished after waiting a further hour and half of stage by stage getting closer to the turtle. People were dropping out like flies, retreating back to the tuk tuk driver and eventually so did we after gaining a glimpse of the turtle digging a hole for the eggs. I knew that at this stage it would at least another hour before it started heading back to sea. Better off swimming with them as this experience is unfair for both parties.
title: Only patient people apply.

body: 150people on the beach for one poor turtle!!! Horrible experience, so sad for the animal.We arrived at 8pm, had to pay 1000, wait of course and walk 30minutes at the beach but this is what you have to do for some nice wild life. I did this before in Australia and wanted to do it again. First, no real information about turtles was given before we went to the beach, the people there are not educated how to approach a turtle while digging a hole. So at the end these 150people where lead by our guide to watch the turtle while digging, which actually disturbed her so much that she stopped and did not lay any eggs. POOR ANIMAL!!!! We saw the turtle going back to the ocean, but 150 people still following, with many flash lights and really not good behavior. Please do not support this as it seems to be nothing else but a rip off of tourist and they actually do not care for turtles!
title: Not worth it! Not turtle friendly at all!!! Do not support this tourist trap!

body: A natural preserve project definitely worth supporting. It’s all organised by volunteers and the mass of people getting there every night turns this into requiring a professional organisation, which would however speak against the volunteer approach of the Turtle Conversation Project.So be patient, respectful of the species, and follow the guides’ instructions. They know what they are doing.We were lucky to see a green turtle digging her hole for ponding. She was rather big. We were about 100 people wishing to follow the spectacular event and the guide managed to ‘control’ us crowd genuinely and with all the Sri Lankan kindness. He took us in groups of max. 10 to the turtle and ensured we were not disturbing its important task.If you go please bring time and patience. It will be overly compensated!
title: Literally guaranteed watching of Seaturtles

body: We were quite lucky as we saw two turtles walking back to the sea in one night,Only advise is: be patient as it takes very long,and we had to walk for almost 30mins in the beach to getTo turtle
title: 2 turtles !

body: Well, please also be prepared that the turtles or any turtle for that matter might not come to lay eggs on the night you are there. We were there on a Saturday, did they take the weekend off or was November the wrong season? We waited for three hours in the late evening and then returned disappointed. Albeit with a briefing abiut sea turtles by the manager. The turtles remained elusive that night. However, sharing here some pictures displayed at the Centre and some interesting information. Buckingham Palace is perhaps the nearest hotel to the Turtle Watch, a 5 minute walk and Ananthaya Beach where we stayed (a lovely boutique hotel by the sea) was about 10-15 minutes by tuk-tuk which the hotel had pre-booked for us and it waited to bring us back. The Turtle Paradise Sea Food Restaurant (A Village Eatery) takes about 10 minutes on foot, a nice option if you start feeling hungry during the watch.
title: The turtles did not come a-visiting!

body: After an half hour waiting in the turtle centre, the guide found a turtle. We went to the beach, looked how she dropped the eggs in the selfmade hole, after she covered them with sand she went back to the sea. The next night, our guide has told us, there were 150 baby turtles crawling from their nest into the sea. So sad we missed this!Nice experience!
title: 3 hrs fun during the night

body: Had read and researched so much about Turtle Watching at Rekawa and that it being a very organised activity, being run professionally by the locals, that I was really excited to visit this and almost pictured a Turtle Crawling out of the Sea to lay the eggs! But as luck would have it, no turtle came that night! We reached here at 8 PM and waited till 11 PM without luck! I somehow got a feeling that this could be a bit more organised as in the nearby hotels taking some initiative and getting information from the Turtle Conservation Project Center over telephone as to the sightings. Because the person at the Center told us that this was not a very high season and there has been no sightings for the past 2 days! But of course we were given some interesting insights regarding the Turtles as to the many different varieties and their characteristics. A better time to visit is in December or later in the year! Also over the years the population has slowly diminished!!
title: Aah! Missed the Turtles!

body: We were very lucky and within 5 minutes of arriving a call was made that we could all go to the beach to see a turtle. It was amazing under the midnight moon and the staff all seemed passionate about the turtles offering time to talk whilst waiting. A cause worth supporting and a great experience.
title: Amazing to see and worth supporting

body: Staff were very knowledgeable,allowed hands on with the baby turtles. Talked about conservation efforts, and how they were managing.Very informative
title: Conservation plus

body: It was new experience for us. We never seen turtle eggs. But it was little expensive. Charges they charged for ticket.
title: New experience

body: Great to see a community organised and caring for the environment and wildlife. Our guide took us to the beach only when the turtle had made its way to the nest sight. Very strict about torches and disturbing the turtle.I felt we were able to take a look without disrupting the nesting process.
title: Worth the effort to go out at night

body: We got asked from our hotel if we would like to head along the coast to go turtle watching at night not realising what it would entail.We arrived about 8.15 and waiting 45 Minutes in the waiting area before heading down to the beach. We walked about 20 minutes along the beach and sat on the wet sand for one hour waiting for go ahead to see the turtle there. Fair enough the guide was waiting for her to start laying her eggs but after an hour in the dark (I actually fell completely asleep in the sand as it was quite late) he gave up waiting and we went over to see her digging her hole. This was very impressive but the hour wait in the late was not worth it and not what we were expecting. The guide asked us to wait and said we will walk down the beach further to see more but it was already 11pm and we were far to tired and fed up of waiting for go and see more so we walked back.
title: Not worth it

body: We were lucky enough to pull up in our tuk tuk at 8:30pm right as it was announced that 'a turtle is on the beach' - so no waiting, though I understand some nights it may be 11pm or later before a turtle arrives. (Note: our evening was a half-moon night with almost no cloud)After paying the 1000 LKR each, approx 20 tourists (this number will vary greatly) are given a very serious and no-nonsense instruction about not using any white light or flash photography. (Red light is ok)We walked down the beach about 200m to find a 150kg Green Turtle high up on the sand in a large hole it had dug and laying eggs. In small groups our guide let us view the egg laying, illuminated by his red-light torch. I suspect the scouts knew about the turtle on the beach for a while prior to allowing us tourists onto the beach in order to both time the viewing of the egg laying and ensure the turtle is settled and committed (which, if this is the case, I wholeheartedly agree with).After the egg laying the turtle spends about an hour laboriously covering the nest, it is exhausting just watching and the effort by the turtle is palpable. The turtle then takes about 20 minutes or so just to haul itself back to the ocean with many bursts of pushing and resting. It is clear that the whole exercise brings the animal to the very brink of complete exhaustion. During this 90 minute odyssey barely anyone other than the guide spoke and perhaps another 15 or so late arrivals joined us. Not a single word was spoken as we shadowed the turtle back down the beach. As the waves finally washed the turtle away into the dark sea the mood was a mixture of joy and relief. If this sort of Eco-experience floats your boat then I'm certain you will find it one you will never forget and well worth a long evenings wait. Some may criticise that the conservation practices are not world standard enough, but we felt that the respect for the animals and the dedication by the (volunteer) operators to put the welfare of the turtles at this stretch of beach absolutely first - was un-reproachable. Especially given the available resources and limited governmental funding for turtle conservation.
title: A special experience

body: We saw a Loggerhead turtle bury her eggs and head out to sea. Our expert guide said we were very lucky. It was a beautiful sighting, There were a lot of people that night on the Watch, but not a problem as the guide knew how to handle all of us and separated us into groups of 10 so that we all got to see the turtle.
title: Lucky

body: The turtle conservation project helps visitors to see these endangered creatures while ensuring the turtles are not disturbed and the environment is protected.We met at 8.00 pm at the visitors' centre near the beach, and were briefed by our guide on not using white light or camera flashes, which disturb the turtles. There were no guarantees that any turtles would come onshore while we were there, but the guides monitor a long stretch of beach, and call each other when a turtle appears. We were in a group if around 25 people, but all observed the guide's instructions to not use lights, and give the turtles space.Our guide led us onto the beach, where we were privileged to see a green turtle laying her eggs, then covering the egg chamber with sand. After resting, she turned and made her way back through the big surf and out to sea.The project is well run, and does a good job of balancing protection with enabling people to see a very special aspect of nature. When we visited, two students from Sri Lanka's Ocean University were carrying out a PhD research project on how to protect the local ecosystem. The involvement of the university, local community and government bodies should help to ensure that the turtles and the whole coastal and marine environment are well protected.
title: Turtles protected

body: We were lucky that a turtle came on the night we were there and we watched her laying her eggs and covering them with sand before struggling down to the water again. There were quite a lot of people but despite this it was well managed and a wonderful experience.
title: Amazing

body: The guide does not explain anything about what kind of tourtles are approaching the beach, they just charge 1.000LKR.Even worse,we were 30 people, most of them bringing PHOTO CAMERAS WITH FLASHES! And the guide touched the green tourtle. It is a pity, they should learn a lot from Tourtles Conservation in Costa Rica. I do not recommend the visit.
title: All fake, only business

body: It is beautifull to see the big turtle strugle in the sand to make a whole and lay the eggs. It is an impressive animal.The other thing is that there are many tourist and the guide is not friendly.
title: Mixed feelings.

body: I was fortunate that when I visited there was only a small group of tourists. Within an hour of arriving we were informed that a green turtle had come to shore to lay her eggs. We walked a short distance across the sand were able to see her tracks from the water to the sand dunes. The guide held the group back until she had laid her eggs (this was approx an hour wait on the beach but it was a beautiful night and just relaxed on the sand while waiting) and than organised us into small groups to get a closer look. Magical experience to witness the turtle.I also enjoyed the information talk before hand and found the guide to be very dedicated, passionate and knowledgable about the conservation of turtles. He was a little difficult to understand at first but well done for talking to a large group of tourists In English when it is your second language. Also had the opportunity to take part in one of the volunteers PHD study. I found this interesting and it raised some thoughts on how to best protect the turtles and their habitat but at the same time engage tourism. These guys are doing some good work and I wish them the best with their PHD studies.
title: Magical experience.

body: I would have given this an excellent rating if this can be done with smaller groups e.g. 20-30 max. The experience of seeing a turtle lay eggs in the beach is magical but we stood there with at least 100 people In the dark with very poor communication, the rushing waves of the sea in the background. Our girls (age 7 and 9) were intimidated by the number of people. In the end we sat in our beach mat a bit out of the way and waited for an hour or so. That was nice actually as we saw the stars and could relax a bit. We left early as the kids were getting tired. I probably would have gone (my husband absolutely not) but was annoyed with the lack of communication and the crowds
title: Too many people

body: Here's my amateur account of what I learned: Turtles need about 2 hours to come to a beach, dig a hole, lay their eggs, cover them and return to the sea. They do it at night and lights disturb them. They cannot hear but I imagine they can sense vibrations. When the babies hatch, they go straight to the sea, attracted by reflections of the moon on the water. They are nourished by the egg yolk and swim for 2 days until they reach deeper waters to feed. Their route is imprinted on their instincts/brains and the females return to the same beach to lay their eggs. There are many turtle farms in Sri Lanka. Some even call themselves research centres. There was never anyone available to answer questions on their research. They assured me that the water in the tanks of turtles was clean and changed at least twice a week - it was in some cases definitely not clean - I couldn't even see the turtles so they could not see much either. Nobody could show me the pH or salinity meter for checking such parameters. They assured me that the eggs were buried in their protected hatchery at the correct depth and temperature but could not back it up with a thermometer reading.The eggs are dug up by poachers, put in a bag, possibly left in the sun for a while, swung around a bit on the way to the farm and eventually reburied inside a protected fence. The poachers would otherwise take the eggs to the market. It is all illegal. At least this way some are saved but I don't know if any of them are able to lay eggs.At Rekawa, the whole beach is protected so the mothers and babies have a potentially natural and protected chance of reproduction and life. Read the other reviews though because they are valid. The guide is very knowledgable and passionate. He is difficult to understand but his vocabulary is actually impressive and you should ask him questions - he will tell you all sorts of facts and show you videos etc. On a one to one basis, he is easier to understand. There are educational programmes to raise awareness locally. I enjoyed talking to the guides and relaxing on the beach at night and waiting my turn to see a turtle. The guide could identify the turtle from its tracks. A few tourists are badly behaved.
title: Turtle conservation with more positives

body: Whilst I was I guess one of the lucky ones and got to see a wonderful turtle laying her eggs ,I was immensely saddened and ashamed and wished I had read the reviews on this before attending what can only be described as a " circus ".At least 100 people crammed around this poor Mama turtle trying to lay her eggs.The guide uses red light and you are able to take photos using a red like setting ,because APPARENTLY the turtle does not mind this ??I just wanted to cry- as a mother I could think of nothing worse than having hoards of tourists crammed around me trying to capture that "'Instaperfect " moment.One of the Tuk Tuk drivers asked me " what is wrong miss ,you see Turtle,why so upset?"Of course there are also that handful of " dicks" who refuse to listen and use flash photography as well.If you truly love wildlife like me - don't go .Just donate to a worthy organisation I am going to do that right now.
title: I felt so terrible:(

body: We had the chance to see both the birth of a hundred turtles and the egg laying of a mother. Great Experience !
title: Great experience !

body: My boyfriend and I visited here and were immediately surprised by the vast number of people there (around 100). We were given an introduction by a member of staff whose English wasn't particularly strong and then followed him across the beach. We walked for at least half an hour across the beach without light which made it a bit tricky. When we found a turtle it was a bit chaotic with the guide shouting at us to get into lines either side of the turtle to watch its journey back to the sea after laying her eggs. Unfortunately some people hadn't followed the guides advice of turning off their flash on their camera. We felt as though with such a large group watching one turtle we were intruding on such a magical experience. Everyone was jostling for position which made the experience a bit uncomfortable. Despite this however, it was incredible watching the turtle and I'm sure everyone has the opportunity to see it and take photos. We decided to leave after this and not continue on to watch another turtle laying it's eggs. Overall it was worthwhile seeing but the experience was not what we imagined or hoped for. It would be much better if they limited the group size
title: Mixed feelings

body: Busy event. Started off well with friendly introduction to the place by someone who unfortunately did not speak very good english. Seemed a good organisation well aimed at the preservation of the turtles. Then had to wait if the turtles would come. Unfortunately they did not. However no one ever told us, so in the end we all (some 100 people) just went home after a couple of hours without being further informed. No money was charged.
title: More info would have been helpful.

body: The staff were immensely knowledgable and cared deeply for the turtles. No turtles have been hurt here for the last 20 years due to their devotion. A lovely way to spend the evening, watching turtles laying and burying their eggs before entering back into the sea
title: Lovely experience

body: On the night we visited there were around 50-100 people wanting to see a turtle coming ashore to lay her eggs. Returning to the same beach she was born on over 30 years ago! While waiting in the visitors' centre we were given a talk on turtles, what to expect to see and the rules. There must not be any light - a difficult proposition in the days of phones. This beach is now protected by Turtle Watch - local people patrol the beach to protect the turtles and the eggs and show tourists wild turtles. Unfortunately the English introduction was probably missed by many non-English speaking tourists. As we were escorted in the dark along the beach the Turtle Watch team had to constantly tell people to switch their phones off. Lights put turtles off and they will turn around and go back to sea. I was impressed with the almost impossible task of keeping the tourists under control. We were ushered up to the nesting turtle in small groups to see the egg laying (using red light). When everyone had seen this we were given an opportunity to go back. Once most had left, the few of us remaining could enjoy a much more peaceful time as this huge turtle covered her eggs with sand and set off slowly to the sea. If you're expecting a quick wildlife experience - don't bother. But if you can soak in the amazing journey these wild turtles have made - it's an experience not to miss.
title: Amazing feat of conservation

body: We went on our own (two people) for a walk on the beach around 9 pm and crossed the path of a green turtle going up the beach to lay its eggs.Two people from the Conservation Project yelled at us about money (one should pay 1000 Rs for an organized tour with them) without explaining anything. They then kicked us out of the beach.The project should:1. Communicate clearly with locals and inform them what tourists should not do. We were sent by our guesthouse and he never mentioned to not use flashlights for example (red light instead). On our way back we met locals taking huge groups of tourists. With flashlights, of course.2. Signalize the beach as a protected turtle area and communicate about what to do / not do.3. Instead of charging money for a guy with a red light showing you a turtle that you can find yourself on the public beach, organize educational tours.Good luck, guys!
title: Terrible communication. More about money than turtles.

body: Like many others, we arrived here just after 8pm.There's a small hut with some interesting facts about the sea turtles that nest here at Rekawa beach. Shortly after the crowd builds, there will be a short briefing and quick lesson on the sea turtles and their endangerment. All very interesting information but everyone's there for 1 reason... To see turtles laying eggs on the beach. Unfortunately, the seas were too rough that night and no turtles made it onto the beach. We were the last to give up waiting just before midnight. You really have to bet on your luck here... Our hotel helped us to arrange a return tuk tuk trip and the driver would wait the entire time there too till you are ready to go back. We gave him a little more rupees than the negotiationed price... He did just sit there for 3.5hrs!
title: We weren't so lucky

body: Saw a turtle leading eggs. Very beautiful beach. Guide didn't give much info. Costs £5 per person if u go with a guide but it's on a public- free- beach
title: Saw a turtle leading eggs. Very beautiful beach

body: I have seen many kinds of turtles. There is one box contains 3 or 4 turtles which has special needs. I have never thought that they can face this kinds of issues. We have seen the place which all the eggs are paired. Not allowed to touch though.
title: Nice

body: This would have been an amazing experience, but a word of warning to families wishing to take small children with them... be prepared for very long trekking on soft sand at nighttime, no lighting (it upsets the turtles) and a lot of waiting. It's an amazing place and really worth going to, but in hindsight and if we had known, we would have left our 4 year old behind. Too much, too late and too long- for her. Other than that, fab.
title: Fantastic- just be wary of taking small children

body: Visited the Turtle Center whilst staying at the neighboring Buckingham Place hotel. Basically there is a small center where you can read about the turtles and then you walk to the beach when "spotters" have seen a turtle.Basically a crowd of "10 humans" watch a mother turtle dig a hole, lay hundreds of eggs then cover it up. A process that has been going on for tens of millions of years.To be honest I had expected to be feeling magical about it but I didn't. I felt we were intruding on this ancient beautiful animal. I realized I was there for my benefit not for its.I now would gladly pay the donation to the Turtle Center not to see the turtles. That said the local economy needs the assistance.I much more enjoyed seeing the Turtle tracks on the beach each morning than the above experience. My wife thinks I am being sanctimonious.
title: Wife and I not aligned

body: We were a little nervous about going turtle watching as we wanted to be as ethical as possible in our animal experiences in Sri Lanka.This experience was truly incredible and worth every penny!There was a small group of us and we saw 2 turtles; one was even laying eggs!I would highly recommend this experience!
title: Worthwhile

body: I was very apprehensive given the reviews. I guess we were lucky, there were `15 people max. We got there really late - 9:30pm but there was a turtle laying eggs, I went to pay 2000 but they said kids are free! We walked down a pretty rocky path to a turtle who had just finished and was burying the eggs. We then got told to "hurry up and not walk like a turtle" and went over to another beautiful creature and got to see her laying her eggs. They said, "she cannot hear you" when someone was whispering.I know that is true when they are laying their eggs, but not once they are finished. So, they need to be educated about talking so loud - the guides! Everyone was respectful of the rules, a couple turned on their white lights and instantly got scolded by the guides. I can see how it would be pretty terrible if you had anymore than 15 as even with that many it was hard to see. Once the second turtle finished laying we got told to go back to the first one. We go there and she was almost back to the ocean. Then everyone left. I said I wanted to go and watch the second one go and cover her eggs and go back to the ocean. That seems okay. So we did, and wait we did. She buried herself into a very awkward position and it took over 2 hours for her to get back to the ocean. They need to limit numbers for sure. They need to be less grumpy - the guide was rude. They need more torches. One between everyone and then he said no more and you couldn't see a thing. Don't take young kids, my son is 8 and even he got bored with over an hour of burying action. Any kids younger - it is just inappropriate and there is significant waiting.
title: Must depend on the night...

body: This was a pretty busy and touristy activity and very hot on the evening we went. You wait around with lots of other people for a turtle to hopefully come up onto the beach to lay her eggs, cover them up then make painfully slow progress back to the ocean. Despite all the waiting around and lots of other tourists (I'd estimate 50 people to see 'our' 1 turtle) I'm really glad our family saw this event. Watching the huge leatherback turtle struggle with the hugely arduous journey from the top of the beach back to the sea was a real privilege. We could hear the turtle sighing with tiredness and hanging her head while gathering strength to move her body and huge shell a few more centimetres closer to the sea!
title: Hot and touristy but well worth doing

body: They have great rules to bad they are not followed by themselves! Very disturbing and worrying!! We felt VERY SORRY we went there! 30 people practically standing in the turtles nest while she was laying her eggs!! They hardly left her alone...They even took a baby from an other nest who was not ready yet, to show how it went to the see:-((((( Horrible altogether !! People using flashlight, talking loud, crazy! They said you could only stand behind the turtle, but this animal was completely surround by people with cameras. No respect for these beautiful creatures :(( now it is low season, i wonder what is going in in high season......
title: Not good

body: This is an experience that we have wanted to see for many years, and what a humbling experience, to see how hard the female turtles have to work to lay their eggs. We were in a group of about 80 people, which probably was too big, and may have been better to stagger smaller groups with more infra red torches. However the guide was very knowledgeable and made sure that everyone was involved.
title: Humbling experience

body: Loved this, really beautiful to watch when done with respect.We were shocked with the lack of respect some tourists had concerning the turtles. Flashes, noise, kids running around without parents to call them out.We were of the opinion that they should be more strict: if someone uses their flash on a turtle laying her eggs, he must leave. If a kid tries to touch a turtle and the parents don't say anything, they should leave.Fortunately all these people usually leave once they have seen the turtle for five minutes so the rest happens in total peace and quiet.
title: Very nice once the people who have no respect leave

body: We get to the location and there is a massive crowd absolutely no order to anything. We are taken out to a beach with no explanation with everyone pushing for no reason. The guide makes us all wait while he goes ahead and walks to a turtle he obviously spotted before we got there. For no reason we stand for a long period of time and then guess what? Another group of about 30 people come and join us. They too try and push up to the front all to see one turtle. Yes one turtle. That was the whole experience. We walked 50 ft on the beach saw one turtle with 60 people and paid 2000 rupees. This is a joke and a major rip off. Not worth the time. Oh, if you do go make sure you bring a flash light with a red lens for the 30 seconds you will see the poor animal.
title: What a joke

body: This was quite a nice experience, however be prepared to wait a while surrounded by lots of other tourists.
title: Okay for something to do in the evening

body: This is an enormous privilege and you must go but leave your torches behind. Infra red only. Go at 20:30, it's cheap and the guides are passionate about their work. It's rather hot and wear mosquito protection.
title: Eggs like ping pong balls!

body: What an horrible night! First, of all, the guide didn't speak English. Couldn't understand a word. On top of this, we had zero explanation. We had to pay 2000 rp instead of 1000 each (why?). We were hundreds of people trying to get a glance of the turtle, the guide was rude, pushing us on the sides shouting at us. Awful. We saw 2 turtles laying, which saved a bit the experience but I felt sorry for these animals.
title: Such a rip off

body: There's lots of reviews here that describe the experience quite well. Some people are horrified, some seem to be thankful that there is a conversation effort at all. Personally, I fall into the horrified camp. Not even so much by turtle watch itself, but more by the behavior of the human beings in attendance. Yes, the guide says no flash photography -- which is great -- but do you think those words are heard by everyone in the group of 70+ people? As the turtle was making its way to the beach, at least 3 to 4 flashes must have gone off. And even though the crowd (thankfully) chided these guests properly, every step of the turtles walk was taken while surrounded with the snapping of camera lenses.Who is the animal in this scene? The turtle or the human?
title: Make up your own mind

body: This so called turtle conservation/spotting program felt like a complete hoax. We we're really (in our hearts) hoping for a good experience... but we left feeling sorry for ourselfs and wished we didn't join this tour.Yes, we saw a turtle! And I wished we hadn't! Hundreds of people (they pretend to take small 10 person groups... yeah right) cramming to see 20 eggs for 3 seconds with no information at all. My friends didn't even realise they were looking at an actual turtle, so vast was the crowd and the pushing in the dark. And don't let me start with the guides, it would not be accepted on tripadvisor!One of the worst things I have done in half a decade of independant traveling... please stay away or just donate money for the preservation. We lost it tonight.
title: Simply no, no way, don't go and no

body: I was very sceptical given the reviews as I didn't want to support a programme where the turtles are handled and harassed by tourists. However, this wasn't the case at all and the guide was very strict about flash photography / white light and nobody was allowed too near to the turtle or to touch her. The experience itself was excellent. We got to see her lay her eggs, cover them and make her way back to the beach which took about 1 hour in total. I would definitely recommend going as it supports a great conservation effort and is beautiful to see. It's not really suitable for young children due to a lot of waiting around and there were a few tired and crying kids disturbing everyone. It's true that the groups are way too big (approx 60-70 people) and it's hard for the guides to get them to queue up and wait for their turn. This is more due to people's inability to obey basic instructions and the fact that adults start behaving like spoilt children when they don't get to be the first to see the turtle rather than the fault of the guide who gave very clear instructions.
title: Worth a Visit - I was skeptical but proved wrong

body: We visit the conservation centre website and we thought that they cared about the turtles and help them. We love animals and thought it could be nice to visit the centre and know more about turtles. Unfortunately what we found is this:They take you, together with hundreds of tourist that don't care about animals but about selfies, to the beach. There was one turtle, the guide took the group so close to the turtle that the poor animal, after crawling for 25 minutes to nest turned back when she felt our presence and went to the sea without leaving the eggs. Meanwhile, the guide was following and touching her, she was terrified. There was kids running and screaming around. Pathetic. We were shocked and wanted to leave. Then they saw another turtle that was nestling. He took the whole group where she was (1 meter from) and let all the people (children screaming and running too) come close to the poor animal that was tried to nest. We then left really sad, I felt really disappointed and upset for participe in this activity that obviously disturb and annoy the animals. These animals are endangered and this "conservation centre" far from taking care of them and help them to reproduce, just take money from foreigners and disturb them. If you love animals DO NOT PARTICIPATE IN THIS CRUEL ACTIVITY. Realy bad for animals, no respect at all.
title: DON'T DO IT IF YOU CARE ABOUT ANIMALS

body: After reading the reviews I was very reluctant to visit but wanted to form my own opinion. Happy to say it was fairly well organised. There were about 20-30 people waiting at the centre. Arrived 8:45pm. Didn't have to wait long as turtles been spotted. Guide advised group of no flash photography, no white lights, only use red lights, stay behind turtle at all times. Took us to see two turtles. A couple of people did use flash so I shouted straight away 'no white light' after that everyone respected rules. Our group seemed quite respectful and listened to the guide, on occasion some people wandered towards front of turtle so I shouted please come back and wait this side as advised by guide. The guide was running between a couple of smaller groups so tried his best to manage the situation. There were other helpers to ensure rules followed too. If bigger groups/irresponsible disrespectful people then can imagine would be more difficult to manage. They are trying to do a good job and am sure it's helping conservation. If only it could be managed by a booking system so limited numbers etc. I would be happy to pay more than 1000rupees to ensure this. If you do visit then maybe can also assist guides by politely reminding people should they use a flash or white light or get in front or too close to the turtles to help save these creatures.
title: Pleased to write a positive review.....

body: We turned up just before 2030 and were the second couple of people to turn up. Over the next 20 minutes a lot more people turned up, id say there were about 50 people in total. I'd work a jumper over my playsuit as I'd read on the companies website that females should cover their shoulders and knees but seemed to be the only one that read this and no-one seemed bothered that the dress code wasn't adhered to so I'm presuming it's not that strict.We were given a talk by one of the guides and told that we would be informed when there were turtles to see. People bought their tickets (1000 rupees each) and waited in the seating area outside. There aren't enough chairs for everyone so if you like to sit down I'd say have one person in your group queue for tickets whilst the rest grab some seats.We were lucky that there was a turtle to see straight away. We all walked down to the beach as a group and it was very well controlled so that no-one was using white light which would scare away the turtles. The first turtle we saw didn't lay eggs and went back into the sea but the second and third we watched build a nest. It was magical.Overall I'd say it is a nice experience. You do have to be patient though as there is some waiting around especially on the beach as they only let groups of ten at a time view the turtle nesting....which I think is a good thing as this project is all about turtle conservation, not bothering them with huge crowds of people.The only negatives I would say was from other people not controlling their children, one particular 10 year old had to be repeatedly told by guides to stay back from the turtles as her parents were doing their own thing and paying no attention to where she was or what she was doing.Also, if you can't walk medium distances across sand then this is probably not for you either.
title: A nice evening

body: Paid 3000 lkr and walked away after 20 mins. Too many people (70)queuing to watch 1 turtle lay eggs. Not a wildlife experience at all. Appreciate the need for an economy but would avoid this. Perhaps influenced by a public holiday (Poya) and others may have been lucky on a quiet night.
title: Sad, overpriced, distasteful, exploitive

body: I went along about 8pm to watch the turtles. There are 2 sittings so ensure you get there on time otherwise you may miss out. Turtle had just laid eggs when we arrived so watch the covering up and retreat to see.
title: Turtles on the beach

body: This was the last activity of a fantastic active afternoon. Long night trek down dark beach, surrounded by occasional lightening, to see two green sea turtles. One had just nested and was struggling to return to the ocean. So exciting to watch her successfully disappear into the dark waves after all her hard work. Then was able to watch another in the process of laying her eggs. Kids absolutely LOVED it. Even after the struggle to get there as it was late and the walk was long. I gave this four stars simply due to the fact that the man watching the egg laying turtle was a little pushy. It's understandable that they are trying not to disrupt her which I fully support, but also it probably could have been a bit more informative — perhaps on the trek down, or when you purchase your ticket. Other than that, extremely well worth the visit and an experience that will stay with the kids forever. Be prepared to have a red flash light handy and absolutely no flash photography. I let Mother Nature be the flash and used the occasional lightening to catch some simple photos.
title: Great eco activity for the kids

body: Community based project protecting the nesting and nests of turtles. A great experience . Although many people , visitors have to understand that it is self funded project from the tour fee. Great work
title: Great work for conservation

body: We headed along to the beach on Saturday evening hoping to see turtles. We were confronted with crowds of people very close to the turtles (not the stated 30m) watching as the turtle made its way to the sea. People seemed to forget that this is a wild animal and having been on a safari earlier that day this did not seem appropriate. The guide we had spoke barely any English, making understanding what was going on very difficult. He also smelt very strongly of alcohol which didn't help the situation. Whilst on the beach a younger guy began talking to us- he was wearing the uniform of the project so we assumed a guide. He was drunk and suggested taking us back to his cabana which was secluded and had no foreigners. As two female travellers this made us feel very uncomfortable, to the point of wanting to leave earlier. Made worse with the lack of concern by the people in charge of the trip when we explained the situation after we got back.Overall not a great experience and had we read earlier reviews we would not have gone.
title: Think before you go: especially female travellers

body: We were staying adjacent to the Centre so we went down to find turtles. Very basic 'centre' with cheap plastic chairs and some dodgy models of turtles but its all very 'local'. waited several hours the first night - to no avail. there are no facilities so take water and a torch with a red filter - white light isn't allowed on the beach as it puts off the turtles.The second night we were more lucky and were directed to a laying Leatherback - fabulous experience. We watched 30-40 eggs being laid then the back-filling process and finally the journey back to those crashing waves.
title: Long (hot) waits but worth it

body: This was an incredible experience to go and see the turtles nesting at night. The staff is very profesionnal and explains losts of stuff related to the turtles.
title: A must-do in Sri-Lanka

body: Great evening, saw a turtle laying her eggs and covering them up.Really well organised as many people there but everyone got a chance to see. Not expensive worth every penny.
title: Great project

body: As much as I enjoyed seeing the beautiful turtle I have to agree with a lot of the negative comments on here. The establishment began in a professional way, we didn't experience crowds and were briefed on our behaviour before we went to the beach. However I agree that far too many people are allowed to watch them and in such close proximity. People were told to be quiet and they weren't and no one enforced this rule- some were even playing music on their phones. People also forgot to switch of their white lights and again this wasn't enforced. And then people were touching her - the guide kept ripping down he bush which covered her to leave her exposed and then as she made her way back there were so many people - I just don't think this is how this experience should be conducted.
title: Mixed emotions

body: 1. Don't bother showing up before 8:30pm. You will not be considered first just because you got there early. 2. There will be many other people there.50-100 people on most nights as we were told. Our group was about 70. 3. You wait until the main coordinator gets a call about a turtle sighting. You then line up to pay 1000rs each. 4. With the other 50-100 people, you walk along the beach. As you get closer to the turtle they make you wait.5. Every so often a guy will come around and say "she is digging now" or "she is resting now", and you reply: "oh wow okay." 6. They put you in groups of 10, (more like 15 in our case) and each group gets a few minutes to watch the turtle burry her eggs. You are NOT provided with red lights, bring your own if you have. 7. If you are not a pushy kind of person, you will probably end up in the back. 7. The turtle eventually goes back to the sea and the massive crowd of people watch her and take pictures every step of the way. One women literally stepped on top of me:l. Didn't enjoy the experience. The turtle was beautiful and it was very cool to see her, but it felt very unsettling to have so many people there, staring at her and pushing others out of the way to take a photo. You may want to consider going because it's for a good cause (maybe- I'm a little skeptical of this organization), not because you are going to have a magical turtle experience:
title: What you should really know before going

body: Realy bad for animals, no respect at all.You will wait hours to see nothing but pay 10 $, when they find one turttle it's like 100 people around, that sucks!
title: DO NOT GO THERE!

body: We were lucky inthat turtle had already started living ege when we arrived on the beach . There were a lot of tourists their but in all honastly it was well rrganised geven them to do .It was a great expriouns to us .
title: Great job

body: I am really concerned about the welfare of the turtles.There was about 40 people going to the beach with the guide and it was horrible! Even the simpliest orders like "don't go infront of the turtle" or "keep it quiet" was too difficult to some people to obey!! I felt so bad for the poor turtle who was doing so hard work laying her eggs and covering them while idiotic tourist where there simply giving no respect to the nature and animals! If this thing would work properly there should be more guides (1 guide for 10 tourist) so the animals would be protected against visiting tourists. And what I read about the conditions during daytime...is this really an ongoing functional project which main focus should be protecting the turtles or is it just act?! If you care about animals and their well-being I advise you to avoid this place untill things change to better direction. I would have if I had known better!
title: Really worried....

body: Turtle watch is, in principle, a very nice project! The entrance fees and donations go to people that were former turtle nest robbers and today take care of the nests in shifts, so that the pretty stretch of beach is observed 24/7. Every night, visitors are being given the possibility to wait from ~20:30pm on at the visitors centre, and if they're lucky, an adult turtle might crawl up the beach, dig a nest and lay eggs. We saw one, but it seems she wasn't content with the sand so no eggs but she slowly crawled back. This would still have been a super fascinating and beautiful experience, had there not been some big idiots in the unfortunately huge group (around 40 persons) too dumb to understand the at least 10 times repeated, simple words "No flash photography!!" "Keep the distance!" "Not in front of the turtle!". Several times, there was flashlight, selfies were being taken close to the poor creature, some persons almost chased her. After that, we didn't know whether we wanted to laugh or cry. Please, don't go to Turtle Watch if:- you're not able to understand the easiest orders - you're not able to walk longer distances on the beach at night - you have kids you can't control - you have too young kids, they want to sleep, not wait, at that time of night If you find yourself in one of that groups: Go watch a movie, you can't disturb nature that way. To the guys from Turtle Watch:You do an amazing job, keep up the good work! But maybe you should really consider reducing the group size (say max. 20 with reservation, first come, first serve) and installing a hefty fine for those not obeying the orders. Then people could watch the majestic creatures happily, and not full of compassion...
title: Nice project, but some idiotic tourists

body: We where very lucky because turtles where on the beach when we arrived. We got to see one covering eggs layed and then return to the ocean. Great experience, only downside was tourists to guide ratio wasn't great so we couldn't hear much of what he was saying.
title: Fun experience

body: Turtle watchIt was a full moon, however being mid December we knew we were a bit early for the main turtle nesting season. So we went along fully expecting not to see a turtle.Arrived at the reception at 8.00pm, being glad we brought anti mozzie spray, so were other as we shared it around. A quick briefing took place and we sat down expecting a long non productive wait. So joy and delight as approx 15 minutes later a buzz of excitement as it is announced that a turtle it's on the beach. We cannot go immediately as they wait until the hole is dug before allowing anyone near. We then go to the beach to witness one of nature's spectacles, a green turtle laying her eggs, under a full moon. This goes on for some time, then watching her carefully cover the eggs.Then a emotional moment as you watch her return to the sea, one big breaking wave and she is gone, hopefully to return in two weeks to repeat the process.A memorable evening. Tips. Visit a cycle shop before you come and buy a red rear lamp/torch as white lights are not allowed on the beach.
title: Emotional Experience

body: We enjoyed the experience so much. It was so emotional and humbling to see nature at its finest. We saw one big turtle laying eggs and on the way back we saw many turtles returning to the water. Even though we were told it was quite a quiet night.Prepare for a waiting time, we waited silently on the beach for one hour till the turtle finished laying the eggs. Totally worth the money.
title: Amazing experience

body: The place does'n have enough facilities for the people who are visiting to see the Turtle... Make sure to bring at least water to drink, because no place to buy over there. There are not friendly and they wanted earning money..
title: Money oriented program

body: It's good to know that there is a foundation to protect the turtles in Rekawa but I'm not sure how much the focus is on the turtles welfare. We went 2 nights in a row and we did see both turtles laying and turtles hatching which is incredible to watch. Simply put though, there are too many people in the groups and it cannot be good for the animals welfare. On the second night we were there it must have been over 100 people. I would rather pay a bit more money for a better organised ticketed system which limited the number of people allowed on the beach. When we asked where the money for the tickets went they answered it was to pay themselves. No wonder they try to sell as many tickets as they can and get as many people as possible onto the beach. I would happily pay more knowing that the numbers of people were limited to what would clearly not affect the turtles.Come prepared for a walk also. The turtles could come to lay anywhere along the beach which is a few km long. The first nights walk must have been a good 20 minutes brisk walk on the sand both there and back.
title: Glad they're here but could do much better

body: What a thrill to walk along the beach and experience the wonder of seeing a huge turtle make a deep burrow in the sand, to lay ping pong ball sized eggs and then make the herculeantask of covering the eggs with sand. A true wonder of nature.
title: Exciting and fabulous

body: The conservation center had lots of information about turtles on the wall, which was great considering that we needed to wait there until one of the former poachers turned conservation guards called base with a sighting. While waiting at the base, the rules were well explained and it was made clear that 1000 rupees per person donation was expected. It was also explained that if no turtles appeared the money would be returned upon request.On this evening we witnessed a green turtle lay her eggs; some people stayed to watch her make her way to the ocean again. She was marvelous, and it was evident that this creature was ancient. Her nearly 1.5 meter diameter led our guide to estimate an aged of 50 years.Our family chose to return early due to the rain. Fortunately the guide offered us his red light to make our way back. In the future I would suggest that the beach path be lit with something more visible than the existing dim flashing red light.Our experience that night was excellent. My concern arose when the next day my son and I returned to the same beach. We were told that the nests were guarded by conservation guards, but all we saw were empty huts, roaming dogs and a huge, 2 meter monitor lizard on a turtle egg prowl. I want to support this conservation effort, but they must be more visible on the beach protecting the nests.
title: A magical moment with mixed feelings

body: We didn't actually do this as the price was 1000 rupees per person to walk on the beach and watch a turtle struggle up with about 50 other people. Yes there are people on the beach at night which they say keep a watch on the turtle nests but they are all sleeping! There were no people on the beach during the day when there are dogs everywhere.. We actually saw a couple of guys digging out hundreds of eggs from a tube in the sand behind a fence which is great to protect the eggs but also seemed a bit sketchy to us? Are they taking eggs from elsewhere else to then have them hatch on this particular 'turtle beach'? Definitely do some research and find out about this place first if you decide to go.
title: Money Making Scheme?

body: Stayed at the stunning Buckingham Place hotel which is only a couple of minutes from the turtle watch. It was my birthday & we were lucky enough to witness a big green turtle laying eggs & then going back to the sea. Apparently in high season there can be as many as 300 people on the beach but on our night there was about 60 in groups of approx 15 that were fairly well controlled. Get there by 8.30. Was an amazing experience :)
title: Magical turtle eco project

body: I hope this review helps this foundation. Today we arrived around 2100 hrs at the rekawa building. With no explanation, information or any instruction we directly moved to the beach with 70 other people. After +/- 800 meter walking on the beach there was a turtle who was giving eggs. Arrived at the turtle the leader only yelled to other people that a flashlight was not allowed. In groups with noisy people you can watch the turtle for a minute and you can take a photo. This took 30 minutes and was chaotic. Some people are calling other people are loud and laughing with each other. Then the turtle walked back to the sea, some people almost jumped on the turtle for a picture. Unfortunately a few people still used the flash light. After this the leader said "questions?". A few people asked questions. No more information was given. Walking back on the beach with a full moon was the best of the evening. I hope that the money what the foundation is getting will be spend well.
title: Not good organized

body: After I was assured that they are following strict procedures of watching turtles I went. In the beginning I was glad in one way, cause they were using only infra red lamps but not so amused about how close we all may come.But the worse thing was after the turtle went back in to the sea. They said there were some baby turtles going to the sea at another place.....(How can you know as the eggs are buried deep in the sand??) Then the guide was digging deep in the sand searching for eggs....there were two eggs. I couldn't see but I believed he broke the shells (otherwise how can they stay under the sand if they were already coming out of there eggs under the sand??) one turtle made it himself in to the ocean. The other one was picked up by the guide, I was very shocked cause turtles coming back to the same place every year for laying there eggs. They know this exact spot by making the magnetic field. What the guide did after was far beyond int. guide lines: he let the baby turtle held by several tourist so they could make a stupid picture., after it he brought the turtle to the ocean.....I criedBesides the research centre looks unprofessional, it's dirty and it really looks like a scam.
title: People please STOP!!! visiting this turtle conservation projectp

body: It was absolutely amazing to see a turtle on the beach, laying their eggs and covering them with sand. But the organisation and guides were not very good. We felt rushed to follow a group that already started. When we approached a turtle covering her eggs, people did not follow guide's instructions as they did not know about the importance of not disturbing the turtle.
title: Too many people and to few guides and guidance

body: We were lucky in that a turtle had already started laying eggs when we arrived on the beach. There were a large number of tourists there but in all honesty it was well organised given the circumstances.It will be one of those experiences that you have to go and see for yourself but you may feel slightly guilty afterwards for intruding on what should be such a private event.
title: All in all a mixed experience but one worth going to see

body: I went twice no turtles first time waited 8-11pm There's a briefing in what to do the do and donts You don't pay the1000 rupees if no turtles Second time I went bit later but people had left it was realy realy far for me I'm 45 and have problems with my legs I eventually got there maby 30 ppl in the group I looked at her a little then felt sad that we were there in private moments in this turtles life Then saw the beautiful big creature slip into the waves
title: Solo

body: It was a waste of time as we waited for 3 hours and there were no turtles to be seen.The guide explained briefly about turtles and they did not charge us as there were no turtles.There were too many tourists and little chairs. You have to wait in a dark area enduring mosquito bites.Not really worth with young kids unless you are an absolute turtle lover.
title: Waste of time - no turtles

body: We visited here for two nights in a row- when you arrive you are talked through the conservation work. Then you wait .. And wait ... Until turtles come and begin to produce eggs on the beach. Nature obviously means they don't always come so you can wait a long time. The first night we ended up seeing a large number of turtles hatching and heading to the sea. This was great however, I felt the group was large and the guides weren't able to control all the attendees meaning some were touching the turtles and shining lights in their eyes .. This was a bit of a shame as they should have been removed after being told on numerous occasions to leave the hatchlings alone. The second night we were lucky enough to see a turtle come up the beach and lay eggs. The group was smaller as many had given up waiting so it was better controlled and amazing to see. I think this conservation does amazing work mainly because it doesn't move the turtles at all, just protects them in their own habitat. Definitely worth the visit and definitely worth waiting!
title: Very good work!

body: There is a lot of information about the sri Lankan turtles in the centre. Qualified personnel were there to answers all our questions. Unfortunately some of my family members did not want wait late in the night to get the turtle laying experience. So we were deprived of that opportunity.
title: A place to see Turtles laying eggs

body: Arrived late as saw momma turtle dragging herself back to sea. The staff wanted to refund our fee as we missed most of the activity but we left the fee as they are doing such a good job. We only saw a positive project with respectful people
title: Respectful

body: Visited @ 8:30pm with my partner.We had our own scooter, so we were not subject to the inflated prices that tuk tuk drivers quote for their services.Once we arrived, management demanded a 1000rs payment with absolutely zero explanation of service. I had a huge suspicion this was actually meant to be a donation, but it was portrayed to be a 'ticket event'.Once down at the beach, a dozen misinformed and curious tourists crowded around a female turtle laying eggs in a delicately constructed chamber. Workers cleared sand around the egg pit so we could all see them. They gawked at the large animal with torches and loudly spoke about what was happening.Around 45 minutes into the 'show' another group of 10 people showed up and again crowded around the female in labour. At this point my partner and another couple decided to leave. The experience had a unnecessary and unnatural feeling to it. I attribute the negative experience to misinformed staff and poor management. How can this program possibly help these poor turtles give birth in a natural way? The only positive I could observe from the program was the placing of metal cages over the nests once the mother had left. Thus protected the nest against lizard and dog attacks.Want to see a turtle give birth? Look up Attenborough's special on YouTube, free and far less invasive.
title: DO NOT VISIT - if you care for the animals

body: Beautiful spectacle of beautiful creatures. The only negative aspect is that there are too many people coming and not always respecting the animals.
title: Worth to come

body: We were staying next door, so thought we'd pop in.It is the quieter end of season, so there was a group of 25 or so.There was no real explanation about what to expect or information about the turtles apart from some photography information.Suddenly, there was a call of " turtle on the beach" and off we trudged. We were herded to the L and then to the R. Not really sure what was happening, eventually a huge turtle appeared under the red light slowly trundling off to sea with us tourists in pursuit. It was a magnificent animal and the crowd was well behaved compared with previous posts.Apparently, she didn't lay any eggs, I'm not surprised given the numbers of observers, I'm sure she was aware of us.Many wanted to see the egg laying, but we were happy just to see a huge turtle.I don't think it was well organised, and can't help but question the negative impact of this activity on these creatures.
title: Great to see turtle but mixed feelings.

body: Lead tours of turtle egg laying in the evenings. They have a number to call and see if turtles are coming ashore that night
title: Informative

body: At first we have to say it was a beautifull experience to see a turtle on the beach. We think its a once in a lifetime experience that you will never forget. However, we are not sure if this is the right way to get this experience. We were with around 50 people on the beach with one turtle and it felt a bit wrong. It felt like we chased the turtle from the beach to the sea. Also there were two tuk-tuk drivers coming along and they seemed to be under the influence of something. They were making a lot of noice and using telephone flashlights. And even trying to sell something to another tourist...We weren't split up in small groups like what they tell you on the website and we felt like some people disturbed the turtle by misbehaving and the guides weren't correcting them.
title: Mixed feelings

body: Basicaly I expected this tour on July, 19 - 2016 as a meet with the neture, but in reality I met a hustling and noizy group of people scaring poor turtles, trying to hude away from people...As well as I suspect, local people eat eggs of these turtles, gathering them out from the sand in nights. Just awful. Avoid supporting this project.
title: Just harassment on turtles

body: I went to there in 9.30 p.m. with a local tuk tuk, It's not very crowd but around 30 peoples are there. all we seen the amazing turtles laying there eggs. It's a very nice thing to see with my eyes. !!!
title: It's a Amazing thing to see !

body: The Conservation Project itself is good and all, but the turtle watch should be more organised.It was just too crowded. We were told that it would be maximum 10-20 people per group, but our group was obviously more than 40. People talked, tried to get to the front to get closer to the turtle, and some were using flashlight although having been told hundreds of times not to (BIG SHAME on those ignorant tourists)! It would be more manageable if the gourp was smaller. Afterall, I personally think that we(tourists) should just leave the turtles alone. Not to go there and cause unnecessary disturbance to the turtles.
title: Good Conservation project, but visitor management needs to improve

body: We were very lucky and a green turtle arrived on the beach to lay her eggs just as we arrived at the visitor centre around 9pm.Turtles aren't quick about this (which is the point) so even when a turtle arrives there will be three hours spent on the beach while the turtle digs a hole, lays her eggs, covers them in sand, and then drags herself back to the sea. A LOT of this time could be spent just sitting on the beach if you are with lots of other tourists!Making a "donation" to a conservation project seems reasonable, but it is clear that this has become victim of its own success and there are now unmanageable numbers of tourists. They could do better crowd control, but that seems to miss the point - it is only to look at one turtle on a beach!It would be MUCH better to limit the number of places to 30 or so each evening, through a booking system of some sort. They could even charge more money per person this way (perhaps a base entry fee and then a "we saw a turtle" top up fee).
title: A victim of its own success

body: Turtles are cute and peaceful animals and obviously this place is designated to orcestrate the flood of tourists approaching the beach. It fails to do soI can highly recommend NOT to go there bec of 5 reasons:1. Though there are good explanations about the animals and their environment in the main station, it was not possible to follow the guides search for turtels or what the were actually doing while the crowd of 150 tourists was ordered to stand at one place for about an hour (we left by then, without seing any)2. The organization is poor. 150 people should be seperated in groups and not pushes on the beach as a rat pac - so you would be able to actually treat the place with respect and observe the turtles in their habitat3. Everyone was asked to buy a "ticket" for 1000 SR. Later it became obvious that this was technically a donation. It is an beach that belongs to the general public. So it seems that the place generates about 1 Mio. RS for every week in off-season. This is a whole lot of money in Sri Lanka. As the place seams fairly underdeveloped i question the use of the money to means of the project.4. tuc-tuc drivers did not like the place either. They make good money with driving us western tourists to the place but they considered it to be sospicous either.5. naive as i am i thought it would be nice to watch the turtels there. With a closer look i must say. Just leave them alone digging their eggs in the sand. Even if you use obly red light for fotos it feels creepy to be there.I decided to at 10pm (without any trace of a turtle).
title: Just don't go there!

body: We arrived around 8.30pm and there was perhaps a manageable group of about 50. However, as we waited for a turtle to be spotted that group grew to over 100. We were told no more than 10 people at a time would be able to see a turtle. It was difficult to see how this would work in practice! When we got word a turtle was spotted the group surged forward to buy tickets - it was chaos! At this point we decided to leave as there were so many people and it was unclear how we were all to be managed.While this is an excellent project, as others have said, they are going to need to start a booking system to deal to the crowd issue. I guess the dilemma for the project is that by doing that it will cut donations (given entry is 1000 rupees pp). However, I don't consider it is sustainable as is and wish I had read the TripAdvisor reviews first!
title: Good idea but crowd control needed

body: Great experience with turtle watch. After a big journey through the deep wood next to the beach we saw a turtle put real eggs and two hours later she went to the sea. How amazing natural experience!
title: Watching turtles at night in rekawala

body: There were about 100 people here the night we visited. (Thursday 4th August), we also had a long wait from 8pm to 10:30 before a turtle was spotted. I realise neither of these things is their fault.When we eventually went to look the size, and behaviour of the crowd was very poor (again not their fault.) I think they should limit crowd size by only selling advance tickets (via web site?) They doo seem to be trying to do the right thing but I think we were unlucky.
title: I think we were unlucky it was very busy
