body: I was a little sceptical before going there. In the end all my bad expectations became true. We started to go there and it was not sure, if we will see a turtle or not. We waited more than two hours and it was so crowded. There were around 50 people, the day before more than 140. We started to walk to the beach, the stars in the sky were amazing. I had to look more at the sky than at the turtle. The turtle was moving away, 50 people following her.... well... this is what you can see. The money could have been spent better and for those who say, the money goes to a good project.... you are right, I agree. But all the tourist harm the turtles...
title: Not worth a penny

body: Really enjoyed our evening.Saw one turtle laying eggs... Absolutely amazing seeing 000's of years of nature.We highly recommend They are doing super work.
title: Excellent

body: Hopefully, review readers will be reading this perception and others before visiting turtle watch. We regretfully did not. Our perception is very similar to the other reviews in terms of Turtle watch's organisation of the evenings events. The concept of Eco tourism is a delicate balance of tourists wanting to witness natural wonders of the guest country versus local communities benefiting from the monetary input of visitors. Turtle watch do not appear to be facilitating this balance. Our visit saw turtles being seriously disturbed by both the tourists and organisers actions. Unbelievably, one organiser stated the obvious by stating " The turtles are not laying eggs because there is too much disturbance". Our actions were akin to trampling through a field of rare orchids or an egg laden Tern colony. It is tempting to think in sinister terms especially when organisers are taking 2000 rupees from each person plus Tuk Tuk drivers are also benefiting from the tourists expectations. Sri Lanka relies heavily on the tourist's purse. Turtle watch methodology to source this money is questionable to say the least.I feel that the only solution to get the balance more favourable to the creature that they are trying to save is more sensitivity to their natural behaviour.Night Vision remote cameras with feeds into the visitor centre would help. This would allow the turtles to nest in peace.Tourists should not be allowed past a perimeter line and should have the use of night vision monoculars. Therefore, visitors numbers to actual site should be limited. I feel that if something is not done to change the organisational practices of Turtle watch, then the creatures will cease coming to these wonderful shores. If people who have visited are sufficiently concerned, they can write or phone the Sri Lanka Wildlife Conservation Society6/5 Kanatte Road, Udahamulla, Nugegoda 10250Phone: +94-72-999-9520 John O'NeillJuly 2016
title: Conservation concerns

body: This could be a great attraction, but is sadly ruined by extremely poor management, extremely poor parenting and sadly quite a few idiots with no care for this planet. When we arrived we thought it was a nice lovely small group of around 10, however we went to the beach and we joined another group to make a huge group of around 70 or 80 people. The management is so poor that these groups are not split and they do not explain the rules. When we were shown a turtle there was a huge rush to get to the front with pushing and shoving. It says no flash photography and people continued to use their flash even after outrage from others. Some people also decided to bring young children who were bored and even decided to run up to the turtles and touch them (parents please don't bring your children if they are not emotionally intelligent or you can't control them). In my opinion this causes distress on the turtles who are surrounded by idiotic humans who can't understand simple instructions. This should not be allowed to continue until the management improves, group sizes are made smaller, photography is banned and also children banned. Please think about the impact we are having upon these turtles before you attend. I left with a sour taste in my mouth and regretting this decision.
title: Why is the world full of so many idiots!

body: Rekawa Turtle Watch is a conservation project that is purely financed by the entree fee tourists pay to be able to see a sea turtle (out of 5 species) lay her eggs and crawl back to the sea. In our experience, TCP Rekawa does this in a responsible way. They make sure that the disturbance of the turtle is kept to a minimum by using only red light and not allowing flash or even cameras that use white light to measure the light conditions. (it is a pity that some tourists need multiple warnings) and letting the tourists keep a respectable distance from the turtle during the part of the process that she is not in her egg-laying trance. We (family with 2 kids aged 6 and 8) were lucky to see a green turtle in a clear and starry night and follow her activities over a period of about 2 hours. Seeing her crawl back into the see and hitting the waves was quite moving. Absolutely recommended, also with kids (6+, depending on their interest in these animals).
title: Moving experience

body: Worthwhile cause. Great value for money and pretty much guaranteed a turtle. Will only charge if turtle appears! Book Ananthaya Beach Resort - next door.
title: Arrive by 8pm but be prepared to wait a few hrs for turtles to appear.

body: We went by bus to Turtle project. Very well run,all visitors clear view and explanation of Turles habits and survival rates. Blown away by the amazing experience. Very cheap as well.
title: Delightful attraction

body: We were so happy with our visit to turtle watch the volunteers were very friendly and informativeWe were lucky and within 5 min of our arrival a female turtle had arrived We waited on the beach for approx 20 min while she dug her egg chamber then the guide took us up in small groups to watch her lay and then cover her eggsThe kids and us adults loved it and commend the guides on a wonderful job
title: Amazing

body: I was happy when my partner told me that we will go to this conservatory and he said that "most of the people are talking about this place", that this place was like the island of sea turtles. Sea turtles come here very night for what reason it unexplainable. Anyhow, to get there was very scary, the road are pitch black dark, cant see anything, no street lights and sign boards are not well recognized bcoz they were small. We reached the place saw some tourists in the main entrance waiting for the guys who were in the beach searching for turtles. A few hours of waiting a guy came and explain the Do's and Dont's. We went inside the beach and its again pitch black, nothing to see, cant use light bcoz its not allowed only the tour guide used ine red light for more that 20 guests. Imagine that!! We walked like more that 1KM to reach where the poor turtle was. The turtle was only one and can't even get a nice photo for remembrance bcoz its not allowed to use camera with flash. Very dissapointing. If the people were talking about this place that sea turtles do come to this place more often, why waiting for more than an hour. Somethings maybe goin on inside the beach and guess what with this dissapointment we paid 1000 rupees to see ine sea turtle. Thats it. Nothing follows. The tour guide said after that thats the turtle for tonight if you want you can go, to those who want to wait to see more they can stay. Its really not worth to visit the place, all you can get was dissapointment. Its much better to visit the turtle farm, take pictures with the baby turtles and adult when the sun is most high, no need red light, you can even play with them and touch them. And if you are very lucky, you can witness the baby turtles released to their natural habitat. This place was a joke. They just make something for money. Not recommendable.
title: Very dissapointed trip

body: Upon arrival, you will be waiting in the turtle information centre. About two hours a turtle had been finally sighted at the beach and everyone had to pay (i.e. you only pay when you see a turtle). It was such an amazing experience to be able to see turtles in the wild! We saw two turtles that night, although none of them laid eggs that nights. Might have been due to the conditions of the sand, or the 20-30 people surrounding it (although the guides try to ensure that people do not get to close or use cameras with flash lights).
title: A night to remember

body: You wait in the project centre until the volunteers find and judge the time right to allow visitors onto the beach to watch. No white light or flash cameras are allowed - illumination of the turtles on the sand is only from red light sources controlled by the volunteers. We were fortunate to see two turtles on the beach when we visited. If they don't judge conditions to be right, the turtles won't lay their eggs and will slowly drag themselves back to the water. All in all, if you would like to see turtles coming ashore to lay their eggs, then this seems to be an ecologically sensitive place to do so.
title: Controlled turtle watching to minimise impact on the turtles

body: Helpful to cobserve the turtles. Although sometimes many tourists.. But worth supporting as at other places the poachers will collect all eggs of the turtles. Definitely go there and support that project!
title: Good project

body: something different, it was wonderful to see how they bring them from the beach and look after them for 3 days and then release them back on the beach, we got to hold a small turtle to hold also a massive one certainly a day to remember.
title: a fantastic time

body: I personally found the turtle conservation project very impressive. Its nice to see how efforts are being made to protect the turtle species. Watching the turtles in their natural habitat where they come in to the shores, dig holes and lay eggs, was indeed a unique adventurous experience.
title: Great Experience

body: details of the trip can be found on their website. at the centre, there is a lot of information on posters about sea turtles - very informative. our group that evening consisted of about 20 people. they didn't bother to separate us into groups. just after 9, we were told that a turtle was digging and that we could go to the beach. when we reached the beach, we were told the turtle had stopped digging as she was not satisfied with the location (common and normal occurrence) and had moved further inland into grassy lands. so we waited... and waited... thankfully about 20 min of waiting in relative silence and darkness (no lights allowed), the giant green sea turtle decided to move back to sea. once it had passed us, we were allowed to follow it from behind and watch it. the staff use red torches (flashlights) to illuminate it so people can see. if you are to bring a torch remember to bring one that has red light. we watched the turtle slowly move back to sea and get carried off by a wave, and were able to take photos (without flash) and videos. the process was over in about 5 min and we each paid 1000 rupees for it. some people stayed on to try and wait for a second turtle, but we left after that. our experience was good. I think May is a good month- turtle peak season and tourist low season. a lot of waiting in patience is involved in this activity but overall i consider it a well organised and meaningful experience and I don't think we disturbed the turtles much given the proper control by staff.
title: worthwhile experience

body: A once in a lifetime experience that is not worsened by the fact you are experiencing it with a large group of other tourists at the same time.
title: Incredible experience

body: Avoid going there ! After waiting an hour in the dark on the beach without any explanation, We were more than 30 people following a turtle who were going back to the sea. How can they say they protect the animal like this !
title: A shame !

body: This was totally disorganised and a total waste of time. I left the evening feeling sorry for the poor turtle.We arrived and were told that we'd be divided into groups of 10, this didn't happen and 70 or so tourists stood around the turtle all edging too close and peering over each other to get a peek. Only 1 guide spoke any English and he didn't tell us what was happening, so we sat on the beach in the dark whispering to each other trying to guess what we might be waiting for. Some other tourists took photos with the flash on - shame on them.This shambles need to be brought under control.
title: Simply appalling

body: Make sure you are visiting the site on the right season. Usually it last till April. Call the visitor centre, it can helps to understand the situation. We arrived there around 8/9pm the parking was already busy with many Tuk Tuk. The agreement it’s usually that they drive you there and wait for your return, which made us feel a little bad, but so it works. We have been escorted to the beach under a beautiful moon light. We were 40/50 people, too many for the only two guides that were meant to have control on the situation. It’s easy to imagine how things may go wrong with larger groups. Lucky enough our group was quite respectful, and in two hours we managed to see two turtles nesting… Yes it is beautiful, and they say turtles can’t see the visitors if they are dressed in black…. Truth is that few people were wearing dark cloths and in any case if the turtles do not see us they certainly can hear us, and this for sure can freak them out. I am not sure that at the centre they have enough personal to watch after more than 20 people at a time. Said so in Sri Lanka it is possible to spot Sea Turtles quite everywhere in the south, so it was our experience… What we experienced with whales watching or turtle watching in Sri Lanka is that in general there is no balance in contenting the tourists and protecting the wild life. They still have to work hard to find the right method. Would be much better to introduce some restrictions and regulate at best the flux of people… It is very sad to have the feeling of disturbing such an old mum like the green turtle…
title: Great Watch Site, Please Be Respectful to Turtles

body: Had high expectations for this, but got bitterly disappointed with how badly the whole thing was organised: couple of guides trying to herd 70 or so ignorant tourist on a dark beach without proper explanation of what was happening. Most visitors had absolutely no respect towards the turtles or the conservation project, and were there apparently just to take some photos to show off to their friends. The guides had no way of controlling what the people were doing, meaning that the only turtle that we truly saw seemed stressed out to say the least (decided not to lay any eggs), and another one turned back without even coming ashore. For those who want to help saving these amazing animals, please, do so by just donating some money.
title: Made me sad

body: This is was a wonderful experience. We saw green turtles laying eggs, covering the eggs and leaving for the ocean. Quite well organized.
title: Incredible experience

body: We wanted to go see the Sea Turtles, and I'm glad we did but I wish we'd known what we were signing up for. *You will be herded out with 50-60 other tourists onto a beach in the dark at night. * You will walk over a mile on sand, in the dark. * You will walk for 60 minutes (round trip) and have to wait idly for 2-3 hours to see the turtles do their thing. * It was VERY hot even at night--no breeze, we were all sweating buckets and actually felt ill at the end of the night. * Some tourists won't listen and will snap photos with flash or get too close, the local guides will yell at them and make the whole thing rather unpleasant. * If you're lucky, you'll catch a glimpse of the turtles laying their eggs, but it will be brief and they have to parade 50 tourists in front of the turtle without freaking the turtle out. Overall - this isn't the most respectful thing to do to the sea turtles. I'm sure they'd prefer to just be left alone. I feel very torn -- it was exciting to see these giant creatures in the wild, but I also recognize that I perpetuated a questionable form of eco-tourism. Research shows that this project is doing nothing to help repopulate the turtles. In fact it could be harming their numbers... DEFINITELY DO NOT BRING CHILDREN. We saw some people bring their kids, and both parents and children were miserable. You need extreme patience for this excursion. Even the adults were bored sitting on a dark beach in silence for 2-3 hours.
title: Know what you're getting into....

body: I am not sure that I have been to the same Conservation Project of the people that have rated the experience 5 stars. If you are thinking about going, imagine this: dozens of people sitting in an outdoor space for almost 2 hours with little if not any explanation about the project, all waiting for a call from "someone" at the beach to spot a turtle. Once the call arrives, everyone is "invited" to pay the 1000 LKR before rushing down to the beach looking for the poor turtle. Once spot, all the "rules" (don't speak in a loud voice, do not use other light other than red light, no flash, do not approach the turtle etc) were completely forgotten. People rushing down the beach, trying to get a glimpse of the poor animal, pushing among the crowd (because yes, it is a crowd), loud noises, flashes. A shame and a complete disappointment. I left with such a bad taste in my mouth that I wished I hadn't seen the turtles at all.If this is conservation....good luck! Avoid.
title: What a shame that such a project is so poorly organized and managed

body: I arrived at 9pm was asked immediately to pay 1000 SkR which was fine then I was told to join the group with no introduction, followed some people down to the beach in the dark followed everybody else and then after about 0.5 km found there was a crowd of 40 people talking and jostling in a place. A man shouting keep back away from a turtle which was digging.I sat down at the she of the group and saw a dark shape starting to come out of the sea about 10 metres away. After some 5 mins a guide saw it and then told me and everyone else to go back to 20 metres away. It was mayhem with people talking and disobeying etc.Then after another 20 mins suddenly lots of people rushed to see the first turtle come back down the beach - far too close and disturbing it with photos and talking.The 2nd turtle turned round and went back. Neither turtle laid eggs because I think they were disturbed by everything.After that there were no instructions and different people went different ways.Little organisation and not good treatment of the turtles!
title: Applaud idea but not well done

body: We saw a huge sea turtle lay her eggs. After a long, hot wait at the beach we rushed down to the beach. It was a very very long walk to where the turtle was (hard for young kids and older people, but well worth the walk. We saw her lay her eggs, rebury them and finally when the turtle made her way back to the sea. Fantastic! Worth the wait but very tiring and not recommended for young children. Bring water and some snacks! Tuktuk from tangalle is 1500 rupiees and for that amount the driver also wait for you and bring you back. We went with our scooter which was fine but we had to ask for the way. Price per person if there is a turtle om the beach is 1000 rupees - if no turtle the admission is free. (but they gladely take donations). It open 20.00 but you can arrive around 20.30. Then the wait is at least a little bit shorter. Absolutely no flashlight allowed (disturbes the turtle) so test your Phone/camera before going to the beach.
title: Worth it! Sea turtle in action!

body: This was a terrible expereince. I, and the rest of my familiy is very close to calling this animal cruelty. This place has no respect for the turtles whatsoever. The amount of people allowed near the turtle was way to big and must have stressed the turtle. The Sea turtle is a threatned animaland the population is falling drasticly! The guide was HORRIBLE! He did not care one bit. He did not tell us what was going on. He did not tell os anything about the turtles. He was way to busy speaking on his cell-phone! All the tourists was respectless too! I can not reccomend this to anyone! Especially to people who care just a little bit about animals we-being.
title: Terrible experince

body: I am a conservation biologist and I thought I would check out how conservation of turtles was done in Sri Lanka. I was so appalled at how the tour was run and actually felt embarrassed to be a human. There was next to 100 people crowded on the beach waiting to watch the turtle to return to sea. When the turtle began its journey back to the ocean everyone crowded around her, giving her no space. People were not meant to use flashes but a few people still did. People were also shouting and not paying any respect.I stepped right back and just wanted to leave as the poor turtle must have been scared. If they continue to run tours in big groups the turtles will be scared off coming back to the beach to nest. We saw hatchlings which was very lucky.. but people had no respect for them and were right in their path back to the ocean. A local was shining a torch on them as he thought this would attract them to the ocean. However artifical light can actually scare them away. People were all over the beach where the hatchings were crawling and not even looking at where they were stepping.I would not recommend going to this place as I think it is run for all the wrong reasons. Conserving animals should be about leaving them be and not scaring them.
title: Not conservation, so disappointed

body: Come and watch the turtles lay their eggs, more importantly, ensure these turtles are cared for. As long as the profits keep rolling in through conservation, the locals will continue protecting their income. We saw a number of turtles lay their eggs, a great experience.
title: A great experience

body: We decided to go to the turtle watch because it is a part of a conservation project (read also the text in the Lonely Planet). When we arrived, there were a lot of other people, between 50-70. After a while 1 turtle was spotted on the beach, so the whole group (!) could come and see. When they saw the turtle, the whole group was standing around it...the group was so big that the local people had no control over it. Only 1 guy was trying and the other helpers were just saying: "enjoy the show"...The turtle didn't put her egg's in the hole on the beach, probably because she was disturbed by us. A lot of people were still using white light (only red is aloud). The whole group escorted the turtle into the sea...It was the most embarassing thing i have ever done...this isn't about the turtles but about earning as much money possible at one time (1000rp per person)!The lack of organization and protection of these animals was painfull to see...i can only say: please don't go!! It's in no way a benefit for the turtle!
title: Don't go there!

body: we went there to see the turtles come asore and lay their eggs.This happens at night time and we were brought to this conservation poject meeting point at 8. 30 pm.After one hour the first turtle came ashore and we could watch her laying eggs ( 120 eggs ! ) . Was a great experience !

Hundreds of tourists were at the beach, loud and disrespectful with their mobile phones and lights. The "ranger" was running around with his flashlight just 1 meter away from the turtle that was laying it's eggs. He was talking as loud as this would be not something, that he should protect as a ranger. All the tourist were really close to the animals and there was no one taking care of anything.Just a sad and expensive experience.I really hope that the locals start someday to think about their environment and try to make money with good things and not with destroying the nature!
title: Sad experience

But there where more People coming! At the point the tour started there where like in 125-200 People!!! There where children screaming, People talking loudly. As you will understand the grouPs where more like 20 People and every body Who was waiting was pushing to be first in line to see the turtle. Again really the worst experience in sri lanka! We watched the turtle digin to lay her eggs and that was very cool. But its really not worth it because I think the watching harms the turtles!! Some man told me the turtles used to lay eggs on the beach, but because of al the People its laying eggs in big holes under the bushes.DONT DONT DONT DONT DONT GO THERE! Unless you like watching anoying People!
title: Worst experience in sri lanka!!!!

body: The turtle watching is simply amazing! It takes about 2-3 hours in total the turtle to lay the eggs so you have a time to watch. The guides are very nice and know a lots of interesting facts. You just probably will not have any good pictures because the turtle can not be disturbed by flash, so just observe and enjoy the natural miracle ;)
title: Exceptional experience

body: The volunteers at the conservation watch appear to be making some fantastic efforts to support the survival and breeding of turtles. When you go to visit in the evening, you will be taken along the beach to see a turtle come into nest (or release eggs back to the ocean). It is not a hatchery, which are present in other areas. The guides were very helpful and willing to answer any questions. Please don't use flash photography (red lights only) and stand behind the turtles. Also, turtles can't hear you speaking, so you don't need to whisper ;)
title: Observation only

body: The staff were bored and seemed more interested in donations than anything else. Once we knew that we were unlikely to see any turtles arriving from the sea to lay eggs, turtles conveniently started to hatch from one of their protected nests. This was very suspicious. They actively encouraged people to hold the hatchlings and take selfies. Handling sea turtles is in the top 10 cruellest wildlife attractions as compiled by World Animal Protection. Make up your own mind if that means they are protecting this species.
title: Not a good experience

body: Very interesting place. We learned a lot about the conservation efforts. They advised us to go snorkelling a hikkaduwa: we saw 4 huge turtles there close to the beach!
title: Highly motivated and knowledgeable staff

body: We arrived at 20:15 ( better not be later than 21:00 or you can miss the show), at around 21:15 the watch in the beach called for a green turtle laying eggs. We all went to the spot guided by one of the volunteers, after a kmoffast walking in the sandy beach, in a beautiful full monlighted beach, we've reached the spot and saw the big carapece at work. It was touching. All our questions were answered kindly. The visits are planned in order not to disturb anyhow the turtles. Very interesting indeed.
title: A very sweet experience.

body: This is simply too basic a project. The statistics that only 1 in 1,000 baby turtles survive to adulthood points to us attempting to improve their chances. Seeing 50 visitors there last night means 50,000 rupees (£250) collected. Can't some of this money go towards a hatchery?
title: Needs Developing and Support

body: Don't be totally put off by the other negative reviews. There are definitely improvements on how they manage the experience however for most people it is a once in a lifetime opportunity to see wild sea turtles laying their eggs, in a way that try's to respect the turtles.Importantly these are wild animals they are not performing on demand for the tourists, so when and where they lay their eggs is up to them. The Rs2,000 cost needs to be seen for what it is - the money goes to the staff, who are trying to protect the natural egg laying habits of these turtles. Unlike the turtle hatcheries to the north, they don't pay fisherman to dig up and collect the eggs and bring them to a hatchery, where when they are born they spend the first days in a tank (on display for the tourists to handle) and then are released on masse (for the tourists to photograph). Here they are trying to control tourists and locals for disturbing the turtles egg laying in a controlled way.In saying all that the demand by tourists regularly exceeds their capacity to manage them. They probably should place some limitation on the numbers of tourists or split them into smaller groups. Due to language barriers a lot of foreign tourists do not seem to understand some of the basic restrictions - no flashlights, keep away from the turtles until advised, as well as some common courtesies - like allowing other tourists time to watch & take photos.This however was a wonderful experience and a highlight of our trip to Sri Lanka.
title: Great experience overwhelmed by demanding tourists

body: As per a lot of the reviews, pretty much a rip off. If you think you're going to be in a small group with a guide, you're wrong. A zoo - of people. Must have been 100+ clamouring around the backside of a laying turtle tonight. ~2,000 rupee tuk tuk, 1,000 rupee entry per person. Save your turtle experience for somewhere more organised.
title: Like turtles? Head elsewhere

body: Rekawa Turtle Conservation project is a community lead project where you can experience the one and only in-situ turtle conservation in Sri Lanka. I volunteered the project for some time and can assure that the visitors getting good spotting of turtles laying eggs in the natural environment. The service standards may be poor as it's community lead and this project needs the attention of turtle lovers in the world.
title: A community experience

body: Unfortunately the Staff and guides let far too many people onto the beach and are not strict enough with stopping people using flashlights and camera lights which disturbs the turtles. People seem more bothered about getting a good photo than showing any respect for the turtles which is really sad. If you do go please be mindful of this and don't use bright lights and camera flashes otherwise there won't be any turtles there in the future. Seeing the turtle was a magical experience but the whole thing was spoilt by bad organisation and lack of control. The conservation project really needs to control things better and inform people to show respect for the turtles environment.
title: Sadly not enough respect for the turtles

body: We visited this place thinking it would be small scale and 'intimate'. But it wasn't. When we arrived we were rushed to the counter to pay for our tickets (1,000 LKR per person) and already thought it was a bit busy around us. Apparently we were the last ones to arrive and we immediately left for a 2 km walk over the beach to the place where the poor turtle was spotted. The walk was at a very healthy pace which was good but did not allow you to check how many people were there. When we arrived there must have been 70 people there kept at a distance of 20 meters of the turtle. The guide told something about turtles but this was impossible to follow with so many people there. Then we could have a look at the turtle laying eggs in groups of 10 which actually were 20 people groups since no one listed and the guide did not control this. So you would see hardly nothing. Once done laying eggs and covering them the turtle made her way back to the sea. 70 people following on (too) close foot. Although the guide told us flashlights were not allowed there where plenty of flashes. Too many people, poorly controlled, I feel a shame I went here. So sad for the turtles...
title: So sad for the turtles... Too many people, poorly controlled

body: my driver was also the guide and he was very nice but the place does not offer any info about how long we need to walk in that particular night to see the turtles. It was a quiet hard for aged people to walk in the sand totally dark with no lights ( we can not use blue light otherwise it will damage the turtles). For the price we paid, we think they could offer a small bottle of water for those who wants and tell how long we need to walk. Many seniors were exhaust probably because they didn't know that we need to walk that much without water in the dark and hot weather
title: a bit scary arriving at night

body: After a long 3 hour wait, it was approaching the 'going home' time of 11pm and I was prepared for nature not showing itself this particular evening. At 10:45pm we were all invited down from the hut to the beach so that we'd at least been outside. Magically, 2 minutes later a worker shone the torch 10 meters away and he was digging down to show us 3 turtle 'hatchlings' that we all followed down to the sea. It was very obvious that these turtles had been buried a few minutes earlier to provide a show for us and so that they could claim the 1000 rupee fee from everyone. My partner said that I was being a pessimist until she later asked a few questions of her own. When asked how our money would help the turtles, the head conservationist replied: 'It pays my salary. We get a bank transfer every two weeks from what is collected'.Our conclusion? Don't give them a penny as they are charging money for a natural event. The entire group clearly shared our views as everyone left without paying. I'm hoping they will get the message.
title: Fake turtle hatching

body: The information centre is quite informative and we had a very good guide who was happy to answer loads of questions. You wait at the information centre (arrive between 8 and 9pm) and when a turtle is spotted by a member of staff on the beach everyone pays (1000 rupees pp) and goes down to the beach. On our visit the staff tried their best to manage the visitors - around 30 people - but stupidity cannot be controlled with simple instructions it seems. The introductory talk clearly states that no one should use white torch light (Turtles cannot see red light so red torches are fine), flash while taking photos, speak loudly or walk heavily. Despite these simple instructions one woman still used flash on 2 occasions - which may have cut short the amount of time the turtle laid eggs for. In short I can understand the frustrations with the initiative that other reviewers express however, during our experience it was other visitors not following instructions that was the biggest problem. So if you go be respectful of the turtles. It is a huge effort for the females to get on land and lay eggs - this is more important than your perfect photo!Maybe selfish tourists will never learn............But the experience was still incredible - we got to see a green turtle laying eggs and crawl back into the sea, it was beautiful
title: Amazing experience but the tourists need to be managed better

body: We went there at 9 and first took a look in the small, informative (but old) museum. Shortly after that we were called that there was a turtle at the beach. We were not allowed to have our own lights, the guide used a red light. The walk over the beach was beautifull by moonlight and getting to see the big turtle lay its eggs was marvellous!! A wonderful experience overall... From getting to read the other reviews that were not so positive I can only say that it was somehow frustrating that some people in my group were louder than I thought is proper in this situation. White lights were not allowed and staff members took good care that we stayed behind the turtle. And we could only come to the beach as the turtle was already laying the eggs. So maybe it improved recently.
title: A great experience!

body: I went there with my friend and we arrived about 9pm. Once there we we're told that a turtle was there already and we paid the 1000 R from then it just got worse and worse. The guide run ahead like a maniac, no explanation just running ahead. After 20 minutes I saw 20 to 30 people or so and we got told hurry up the turtle is going back in the water. This was it really, they did nothing at all for the money. The poore turtle had digged a hole but with so many people around and lots of red light on it I am sure it didn't feel safe to lay eggs. In any case I accept this is nature but the way we interfere with nature is no surprise that we contribute to the fact that only 1 in 10000 turtles reaches adulthood. This was a truly unpleasant experience.
title: Terrible experience

body: It's not a surprise that this attraction gets mixed reviews. There are people who love it, because they get fascinated with the turtles but I am not so easily impressed. There is even a review from a guy who said that it is very cheap and suggested that they should double the price. Excuse me. These guys make a lot of money from this "conservation project" business. On a bad day, they get about 30 tourists. At Rp 1000 per ticket, they make Rp 30,000 which is the average monthly income of many families in Sri Lanka. In the high season, when they manage to gather around 200 tourists, they make Rp 200,000 per day. How are they using this money for the conservation project? Did anyone get any feedback on this from them? Has anyone received a pamphlet with information on the turtles or on the project? No. There is little value for the money they charge. We saw two turtles, none of them were laying eggs because they were probably stressed with so many people moving around them. So yes, the turtles are being used for their profit, just like the all the "Elephant Safari" throughout Southeast Asia or the Lion Park in South Africa.
title: It's all about the money

body: Set outside of the city - seemingly the only conservation center aimed towards ecotourism rather than just making dollars for profit, sits Project Turtle Watch. I showed up at a poor time to ask people questions about operations rather than for a turtle walk. I figured showing up at an off time wouldn't have the results I was looking for. That stood true - but I left surprised and happy with the project they are running. Locals are empowered and are running the center on shifts and are incredibly helpful and kind even if they can't speak the same language. And if you can't manage to figure out how to talk to anybody - there is lots of awesome art, great information, and interactive exhibits available to check out in headquarters. If you have some time to kill and want to go on an easy adventure, getting in a tuk-tuk and heading out to Project Turtle Watch should make it on your list.
title: A Good Start

body: We went to see the turtles on the beach and it was incredible. We really enjoyed it!! The man with the umbrella was very knowledgeable. It was a beautiful evening!
title: Amazing experience

body: Fantastic and unforgettable experience. I was astonished to experience a large ses turtle laying her 100 eggs right in front of my eyes. Such a beautiful Think to witness and very intimate. The wait at the Beach with no lighus allowed gives you a wonderful experience with the sounds of Rolling waves, seeing the contours of the palmtrees as some fireflies show up here and there and the milky Way is clearly visible above. Very Nice indeed!
title: Incredible and exttemely beautiful experience

body: The Turtle Conservation Project at Rekawa gets very mixed reviews - I guess it mostly depends on how lucky you are with the turtles. We visited on the evening of 21 August. After arriving and being given a brief introduction you're left in a fairly cramped hut with limited and pretty basic seating and I really wasn't looking forward to what I expected to be a long wait with no guarantee of a sighting at all. But within about 30 minutes a message came through that a turtle was on the beach - and very close by. By now there were about 50 people and after paying our 1000 LKR fee we made our way down onto the sand. We saw the turtle returning to the sea without having laid any eggs - the guide said she had probably been checking the beach and would return in the early hours. Fortunately we were allowed to stay on the beach rather than return to the hut, which was much more pleasant (sea, sand, night sky and fire flies to watch). After a while another turtle was spotted - this was very much a repeat with the turtle returning to the sea without laying. Then our luck really changed - baby turtles were starting to hatch from one of the existing nests. Seeing 25-30 tiny turtles making their first journey down the beach to the sea was an amazing experience. And even this was not the end as another turtle had come ashore in the meantime and dug the hole in which she would lay her eggs - a process we were able to watch. So for us, 3 adult turtles and a host of babies within the space of around 3 hours - amazing! I accept we were really lucky and had we been on another evening we might have seen nothing at all. But this is how it is (and should be) - you should not expect nature to perform for you on demand.Others have commented negatively on the number of people - I can only say that for us the 50 or so was a significant number but all were generally happy to follow the instructions given by the guide who took us in small groups to witness the egg laying - while the turtles themselves did not appear to be unduly disturbed by our presence. And if the charges go towards paying local people to monitor and protect the beach rather than poach turtles as once happened then surely this has to be good for everyone.
title: Magical experience

body: We visited here in August to try and see a turtle lay her eggs. After a long, hot wait we rushed down to the beach as the sea turtle had begun to make her nest. It was a very very long walk to where she was (hard for young kids), but well worth the walk. We saw her lay her eggs, rebury them and finally make her way back to the sea. One of the most magical things I have ever seen. Worth the wait but very tiring and not recommended for young children.
title: Lovely

body: I first visited Rekawa 4 years ago when the turtle project just began. I am so happy to see it is now thriving and sustaining solely off tourism, whereas before it was outside funds. The protectors were once hunting the turtle eggs as a means of income, but now they are taking tourist to watch the nesting turtles. True, it needs some work. I don't think they were prepared for to program to become so popular and to get so busy in the high months. More organization would be nice but keep in mind this project has come a long way and is supporting the local community greatly. Also, the guides have never worked anywhere by "western" standards so they can see pushy and rude- before they were poachers. With that said, I recommend visiting the beach and witnessing this spectacular event by nature all while supporting the local community.
title: Good eco-tourism experience

body: We started walking down the beach around 20.30. Cca 50-70 people. We all had one guide that spoke English and nicely told us about flash, lights and silent talking. But hey, people are stupid mostly, how can you expect them to not flash, even when you tell them not to.But okay, human stupidity is nothing special . We arrived at the spot and had to wait 2 hours, because the turtle's hole collapsed. There was no organisation at all. The guide said : " wait here", and people that were late didn't know any of this, and just walked by. After the 2 hours, we moved forward, and waited for turtle to dig another hole. After the hole collapsed again and turtle started going to the sea, the guide started yelling: " come, come fast to see the turtle". There were 70 people "watching" that one turtle for 50 seconds and at least 10 people flashing all the time, even after everyone telling them not to. And that was it of the night. I've told the guide that i want my money returned because i'm not happy with the project, and that they advertise that you get money back if you don't see the turtle. He said :" you saw the turtle, didn't you?" So that was all the rush at the end about. That everyone could see the turtle for 5 seconds so they could say that we all saw it and not return the money. All they care about is that 1000 LKR.
title: Waste of money and time

body: This experience which starts at 8PM and last 3-4 hours is great, but there are too many people around. We went at nightime and we were 70 people on the beach which were just too many. You get to see mother turtles coming up and digging the holes in which they lay their eggs, but the first 2 we saw turned around and headed back to the ocean presumably because they got startled by the many people. Then we saw them releasing hatchlings into the ocean from their protected nests which was really fun to see, but a few people ended up stepping on a few of the young turtles since they allowed us to come very close and there were no rules set on what we were about to see or how we should behave. The overall turtle conservation initiative is fantastic, but they need to take fewer people on the beach and set some strict ground rules (ie no photography at all would be great as bright lights scare the turtles). The price is 1000 rupees which is cheap, so in order to maintain revenue they should double prices and only take half the people. That would make for a better experience for the tourists and more importantly the turtles!
title: Great but way too many people

body: For a project dedicated to protecting these turtles we were both shocked and horrified by this experience. We arrived to a group of over 100 people and given an introduction speech - which we couldn't hear due to overcrowding, in English which was likely good. Clear rules regarding behaviour made VERY clear. We were herded to the beach in the dark, couldn't see where going/tripping over stones etc. when there had to walk a while up the beach. Then waited for at least 20mins in the dark with no idea what was happening to then have groups of over 10 go to see "something". At this point we had no idea what was going on, when our turn would be etc. and it was a pushing free for all to get in there first. when our turn eventually came (we just sat and waited) we saw a turtle laying eggs at the back of the beach. The guide at this point yelling at us (bearing in mind he was right next to it) to "move on as soon as you've seen it" repeatedly, with increasing volume and aggression. This gave literally 5 secs viewing, of which was feeling guilty about taking too long so you couldn't relax or take in what you were seeing. I didn't like how he was shouting near the turtle either. I assume this was because there were only so many eggs and more viewers to get through. We then walked to the other side of the turtle we waited again for a good 40 mins or so, for the remaining viewers to come through and then we all went back a second time to look again. We decided to go near the end this time so we weren't rushed like before. This time the turtle was pushing its way through the undergrowth to start its way to the sea. The guide this time was pulling and shaking the branches/leaves where it was..for what reason I have no idea, but it wasn't in line with "conservation" and it appearing he was trying to scare it out. We then moved on and sat down - as everyone else was. Again no idea at this point what was going on! We were then shouted at for being too close to the turtle...but we had been given no direction. They drew a line in the sand to sit behind - and we waited. The turtle came out a few seconds later and started its long walk to the beach. This was truly magical and worth the wait!! Sadly at this point lots of people started going over the line, crowding it/following it/making noises etc. this completely blocked the view of the majority waiting behind the line causing further shouting and arguing. Without a doubt it was amazing to see...once we eventually got to after over an hour of stress/uncertainty as to what was happening. Sadly it is an EXTREMELY ill managed event, which is seriously overcrowded. Managing better could involve pre-grouping with number cards/string lines for waiting etc would all help control the masses of people who are basically out for themselves and not the wellbeing of the turtles. The overcrowding makes me question the motive of this organisation. I would happily go again if it was managed better and a maximum of 20-30 people. I'd even pay more for a more peaceful and appropriate experienced for the turtles.
title: Those poor creatures

body: We had a spectacular evening on the beach watching a turtle under the stars. Yes there are a lot of people and at times it can feel a little disorganized. However, everyone gets a turn to see the turtle more than once while she lays her eggs. A lot of people then leave. We chose to stay until she returned to the sea and by the time we left the beach there were only 10 people left. The information centre was highly informative and well presented. The level of conservation was impressive and upmost care was taken to protect these precious animals. The guides were informative and the fact that the eggs are left to incubate in situ makes this place incredable. I HIGHLY recomend this place to view wild turtles. I would come back in a heart beat. Loved the experence.
title: Spectacular evening

body: You get rushed along the beach to end up with a crowd of unorganized people. There you get yelled around by the organizers. "Come here!", "Go away!", "Too close!".Then they ask for "10 people" to come and expect the crowd to organize itself - sure that would be nice but is unfeasible for such an event, especially when it's dark and you don't really know where to go and not to go.Maybe it used to be better when it was less people, but they are in dire need to change their structure. Maybe DO implement a registration process and a waiting list.Pre-group people into 10s (or whatever number seems clever) and have them stick together, give them a group number.They yell around to organize the crowd. Apparently turtles don't hear that. But even if that is the case, human's do hear it. And it feels stressful, unprofessional and kills the mood.On the way back we used our headlight with white light. One of the employees rushed to us and told us to immediately turn off that light, all the while having a white flashlight himself.. lol. Bottom line: the turtle itself was interesting and nice too see. But the whole organisation was just horrible.
title: Horrible organisation

body: Considering this is a conservation project it seemed more about the money. We went to see the turtles and when we arrived there were already 50 people waiting. You wait until the spotters call through to the main building to let you know there is a turtle on the beach. You all then trot off to find it. I understand that this could be quite a trek. Our guide said that this was too crowded and advised we went back the next night. We decided not to but my partner's children did. This time there were at least 100 people waiting. A turtle was spotted but as soon as the crowds went on the beach it went straight back into the water. If you did get to see a turtle you had to pay 1000 rupees (about £5). Times that by a 100 people. £££

body: We were really fortunate in that a turtle came onto the beach just as we arrived. There were probably a maximum of 40 people on the beach and we all took turns to view the turtle. There was 40 -50 people there last night which is far too many in my opinion as then it becomes a stampede and a pushing match to see anything! I was moved by this female turtle as I thought about how she has genes that are 200 million years old and she is being patient with us tourists who are gawking at her and taking photos, all the while knowing that she apparently did not see us.
