body: Though we were at least 30 people looking at the same turtle coming on land it was a fantastic experience. I felt comfortable letting the guys from the project give usdirections as to how to enjoy the turtles without disturbing them. Brought my son of 8. He was very impressed and excited. There is some waiting time and uncertainty to the adventure sonce you never know if a turtle will come, but it was worth it.
title: Great project, interesting

body: We visited from Tangalle by tuktuk - you will need to organise transport to visit this place as it is quite far from the main road. In principle, this project is a great idea – convert local turtle poachers into protectors and get tourist dollars to support the local community. You start at the village around 8pm where a building houses information about the project and turtles in general. The guides also give you instructions as to what to expect – spotters on the beach will notify the guides when turtles arrive and then the visitors will go to the beach. No bright lights, no white lights, no flash, no going near the turtle at certain stages, keep quiet, stay behind the turtle when it is returning to the water. I am sure that this is all sound advice to protect the critically endangered animal. It is great that all of these rules are clearly established before going to the beach. However, once on the beach, the rules were repeatedly disregarded by inconsiderate tourists despite repeated requests from the guide.Our first turtle was spotted after only 30 to 45 minutes, so we all set out down to the beach (40 to 50 tourists). The first turtle was some way down the beach and when we arrived near the nesting site, the group waited at a distance until the spotter gave the signal that the turtle could be approached. However, of the four turtles we saw, three of them returned to the sea before laying their eggs. Whilst this may be due to the official explanation that the sand conditions were not right, I cannot help but wonder whether it is also impacted by the presence of forty tourists trying to be quiet. As mentioned by the previous recent reviewers, then the fun started. Our first turtle was heading back down to the sea after aborting the nest digging. The guide requested that we keep behind the turtle. Whilst this request was initially respected, soon the animal was crowded by tourists, thrusting cameras and phones right up to the animals head, using flash cameras and phones in vain attempts to get a photo (presumably for facebook). Bearing in mind that the beach is in total darkness aside from the moon, the likelihood of getting a photo without a flash is almost zero. This situation was repeated with a further two turtles with the guide’s repeated requests to stick to the rules being completely disregarded. Finally, a turtle decided to lay eggs. There was a long wait (probably an hour) at a discrete distance for the turtle to complete the digging of the nest chamber. Then the guide stated that groups could approach the turtle as it started laying eggs (the turtle is apparently in a trance at this stage so can be approached without disturbing it). However, again, there was little or no control of the crowd and there was a rush to be in the first group to the nesting site. However, the turtle did not start laying eggs straight away and instead of rotating the groups (say every 10 minutes), the guide insisted that the second group wait (probably 30 minutes). One family in the second group had a very young child and there should have been some control to let children approach first. Some people simply gave up waiting and ignored the guide and joined the first group. Finally, the turtle commenced egg laying and the first group very slowly disbanded. By this time, a big lightning storm was approaching and it was beginning to rain. We finally approached the turtle and admittedly it was quite an incredible sight to see it laying eggs into the chamber. So, very mixed feelings about this project. What should be a once in the lifetime experience was marred by inconsiderate tourists and lack of crowd control by the project staff. On the good side, it has converted the turtle poachers into turtle protectors and brings in tourist dollars to support the community. On the bad side, the control of the tourists is non-existent and needs significant work. Smaller groups and a quota for each night would be a good start (a higher price could be charged for the privilege of seeing this miracle of nature). However, the onlookers could also be easily controlled with a piece of rope held by members of the team to keep the tourists away from turtles when they are heading back to the sea. Without some control, I’m not sure that turtles will be returning to this beach for much longer. If despite this review, you do decide to support and visit this project, be a responsible tourist, follow the rules and think of the animals – not your next facebook post.
title: Good intentioned project marred by inconsiderate tourists and lack of control by project staff

body: The walk along the beach on a moonless night is not pleasant. Take a red light torch with you and go. The numbers are too much. May be can be allocated to two guides.
title: Good project

body: We stopped in rekawa for a night to see the turtle nesting and our experience was horrible. We were about 50 visitors waiting at the building, which display some good information about turtles.After what seemed like 2 hours, we finaly went down to the beach, not 10 at a time like mentioned,but all 50 of us at once only to see 1 turtle, obviously too stressed out by our presence. The turtle turned around and went back to the sea without laying its eggs.The people in charge not only brought us too close to the turtle, but even allowed imbecile tourists to take photos with flash while touching the turtle!!! Totally unacceptable...And they ask 10 bucks for this! A complete rip off. They couldnt care less for the turtle. This is a big masquerade. Fyi: im writting this from trincomale, where blue whale watching is half the price asked in mirissa.
title: Pathetic ...

body: This is meant to be a "turtle conservation" project, but my experience was awful because there were too many people there for it to be responsible. I felt like we were disturbing natural patterns, crowding the poor turtles, and incredibly, more than 10 people nearly stepped on small hatching turtles on their way to the sea because it is impossible to see where you are going as so many people are there. Of course, we shouldn't be there at all in reality. If I hadn't noticed that there were turtles underfoot, no doubt someone would have stepped on them. Stay away and do not visit. The next day we were sunbathing and just happened to see other hatching turtles making their way to the sea (during day time) and although I felt again that we shouldn't be there, at least we hadn't paid and it felt more "natural".The tour leader also nearly stepped on the turtles, and did not give me the impression he knew what he was talking about. He shouted a lot and didn't control the crowd properly resulting in an uncomfortable experience where I felt distressed that we were disturbing the turtles. I think the only way this would work is if the tour groups were limited to 10 people, and if the entry fee was raised.
title: Very irresponsible and felt ashamed when I realised the way it worked

body: I think I must have visited on the same night as the reviewer Holly E below, because I had exactly the same experience.I appreciate the efforts that this conservation project is making to protect endangered species of turtles. Having said this, like many conservation efforts in the developing world, Rekawa Turtle Watch seems to be caught in a double bind between following appropriate conservation practices and relying upon income from tourists in order to sustain the project.The project's conservation efforts and the experience of observing the turtles are marred by the very large size of the visiting groups, which makes controlling the irresponsible behaviour of the crowd impossible. I counted about forty tourists on the night I visited. Despite repeated exhortations from the guide to refrain from using lights or flash photography (because white light is distressing to the turtles), several people ignored these warnings. Although I enjoyed listening to the turtle digging, after she abandoned the attempt and began to crawl back towards the sea the crowd of visitors surged forward in pursuit of the turtle. Because most people were holding up cameras (and in some cases using forbidden flashes), it was very difficult for those of us at the back to see. Finally, I was appalled when three or four people walked up to the turtle and tried to push it into the sea. Afterwards, my husband twice tried to bring this to the attention of the guide but he walked away in the middle of the conversation both times.I expected to quietly observe a turtle nesting from an appropriate distance. Instead, I was part of a large crowd of unruly visitors whose sole intent seemed to be to get a good photograph. I left feeling as though I had participated in something that was not in the best interests of the turtles.
title: A well-intentioned conservation project marred by badly behaved visitors

body: I went to the beach last night, and it could have been a completely magical experience. The beach was dark, the sky full of amazing stars and we could hear a sea turtle as she was digging her nest. Sadly, as soon as the guide gave us the go-ahead to come closer and see her, 30 odd people pushed forward. A few of us stood back and watched as the throng almost chased the turtle down the beach, every one scrambling for a picture. No one was enjoying the special sight, everyone was too busy looking through their screens, trying to get a picture to show their mates. The worst bit for me was when 3 or so girls ran into the water to grab and touch the poor turtle as she made her way into the sea. I was so shocked! I couldn't believe they thought it was ok to chase and grab a wild endangered animal like that.Wild animals, endangered animals, are NOT a photo opportunity. Sadly it seemed everyone on the beach last night thought differently.I only wish this special event was viewed as such. Tickets should be more expensive for a maximum of ten people a night. Cameras should be banned. My advice is to go, support this amazing charity, but be respectful. View the experience with your eyes, not your camera lens, and for gods sake turn your torches off too!
title: Silly Tourists Ruined The Experience

body: it is a must to see when you are in ranna. you have to be their by 8 pm . you can see turtle for sure.
title: a thing to do in the night

body: We went on two occasions since we were staying very close by. On one evening we saw some baby turtles bravely venturing into the terrifyingly rough surf. On the other evening we saw a giant green mamma turtle peacefully laying her eggs in the soft white sand. These were both beautiful and magical moments that we will treasure in our memories forever. There were around 25 other visitors who came on the evenings to witness the events. Some of the people were a little noisy and were disrespectful of the rules, which really annoyed us. Fortunately the local guide assertively spoke up and told these people off. This is a worthwhile cause to support because amongst other things:• It has turned the local people who once used to hunt the turtles into conservationists;• The efforts of the conservationists help with the survival of major turtle species (we were shocked that global turtle numbers have been decimated from 2 billion to 10 million);• The donated money goes to the local people to continue their 24 hour 7 day a week monitoring and patrolling of this stretch of beach and incentivises them to not hunt turtles anymore;• It helps to educate the visitors on the importance that turtles have on the health of the world (e.g. stabilising jellyfish numbers). TIPS:• The visitor’s shack is located at the end of some poorly lit dirt roads that run for about 3km. You will need to arrange transport to get there. • You should get there at about 8:30PM but do not expect to see turtles straight away. You may have to wait for a while.• One of the local “lookouts” will notify the lead Guide that a turtle has come onto the beach and is laying eggs. That is the signal for everyone to follow the lead Guide to the beach.• A “donation” of Rp 1,000 (about USD 10) is EXPECTED from each visitor, but only if a turtle comes onto the beach for viewing. You can of course donate more. • Bring a RED LIGHT if you have one. White light use on the beach is forbidden as this disturbs the turtles (this means NO flash photography or use of cell phones or white light torches). The lead Guide will have a red light for his own use. • It is quite okay to talk quietly on the beach, but minimise the amount of vibrations through the ground as this may disturb the turtles.• No smoking on the beach and take all rubbish with you. • If you spot a turtle coming onto the beach, give her a wide berth to avoid scaring it. They spook easily. • Once the turtle starts laying her eggs, she will go into a trance like state and it is quite okay to go near her at this stage. But always follow the lead Guide’s direction.• Total visit time is dependent on when the turtle comes onto the beach. If you are short on patience or short on time or don't really care about the conservation project then this is probably not for you.
title: We saw baby turtles and big mamma turtles – note my TIPS!

body: Not worth the time or money. My expectation was seeing a few turtles come to shore and we sit there watching them lay their eggs. In reality, you're surrounded by 50 other tourists and waiting on the beach in the dark for over an hour. We were told not to use any light or flashes on the beach so that we don't disturb the turtle, but many selfish tourists couldn't help but check their phones for whatever reason. Eventually when we were told that we were able to see the turtle, they grouped us in to teams of 10 so we could get a close look. All you see is the back of the turtle and the eggs for a few seconds. The conservation project should limit the numbers to make this a more enjoyable experience.
title: Disappointing

body: You go to this beach around 7.30 p.m after your dinner .You have to wait for some time and when the turtle comes out you should not make much movement or take photos by using the flasher, till she lays the first egg. Then you can go close to the turtle. You pay Rs 1000 but it is worth. But keep in mind that you have to have a bit of luck to see the full show of turtle laying eggs.
title: You have to be lucky to see turtles

body: Neat experience to see a huge turtle laying eggs. Cool to see different types of turtles painted onto floor of the center. Great talk/video shown to students.
title: Turtle Viewing

body: So many people gave in / gave up! I guess we were lucky as a member of staff at the hotel seemed to have a "turtle hotline" so we only went over when the 1st sighting had been confirmed. Despite not getting back till 1:30 it was absolutely worth the wait. We saw 5 what seemed to be huge green turtles though the guide said the other week there was a leatherback that was over 2m!Although there is dual pricing as the money is going to much needs conservation then I'm happy with that when you consider how much people will pay for just a glass of wine back home.
title: Absolutely worth the wait

body: This is really expensive for what it is (1000 Rs) and you don't even know were the money goes.Explanations about turtles are limited.You have to wait to know if you will see a turtle and after you have to wait to see the turtle, at least 2hours. I know mother nature takes its time but 1000 rs for less than 1min to see a turtle...I will not recommend it, except for turtles' lovers!
title: ONLY for turtles' lovers

body: 'Foreigners' (not tourists, but foreigners, exemplifying the real otherness that seems accepted here) have to pay 1000 rupees, Sri Lankans 150 rupees. I'm just wondering if london attractions started charging foreigners 10 times as much for a ticket how well that would be received?!
title: 'Foreigners' pay ten times more

body: We did not think much of this little trip in advance but it was great! The kids loved it! It is a small place that does not look much when you get there but the girl who guided us around did a great job making each sight and turtle interesting. They are doing a fantastic job with the turtles here! And the beach where the turtles lay their eggs is stunning too!
title: Loved this short little trip!

body: When we arrived on the beach and realised there so many other tourists I wasn't sure whether this was going to be a disappointment. I didn't need to worry this was one of the best experiences of our holiday.The project staff are very careful to ensure the turtles are not disturbed so only allow a few people near them at a time. Once we had all seen her laying eggs the staff gave people the option to leave or to wait another hour to watch her head back to the sea. We decided to stay and in our opinion sitting under the stars listening to the crashing waves and then watching the turtle slowly make her way down the beach was totally worth the wait.
title: Patience rewarded

body: Really good experience even if you cannot see the complet process.Volonteers are very friendly.If you don't see a turtle you don't have to pay, but the money is really usefull for saving the turtles
title: Eco friendly

body: somewhat idealistically i thought we would be able to sit on the beach and watch the turtles come ashore , instead we along with 100 or so tourists were herded onto the beach only to sit there in darkness for well over an hour , the one turtle that was there started to dig and then her egg chamber collapsed , i appreciate that its not a guarantee but with a small child with me it wasnt the best experience ...we left before having to wait another hour or so ...my suggestion to the project is that theyshoudl at least have some food/ drinks available on site particularly given the numbers of tourists attending and the fact that many included families with children
title: Dont bother

body: long time waiting (from 20h to 23h) but we saw adult turtle and also a lot of small turtles going to the sea
title: midnight watching

body: Watch a turtle come to shore and lay eggs in the sand while listening to the waves crash on a dark, abandoned beach, only to return to the waves... magical. The tours are run by informative and friendly English speaking volunteers and experienced locals, the project is run by the born free conservation group and has put together a great (but basic) information centre on the beach, to be perused while waiting for turtles to appear. The centre could be cleaner but is adequate. As with all natural things, a bit of luck and some patience is needed if you are to fully appreciate the experience, but it is rare to see no turtles (even during the less popular months). You only pay for a ticket if a turtle comes ashore. Get there at 8pm and be prepared for a late night, ours ended at 23h30. We paid about 9usd per ticket.
title: Magical experience, if you're patient

body: It was a long wait and there were way too many other tourists (about 100+) people waiting on the beach, but it was absolutely worth it. We not only got to see a mama green turtle lay her eggs, but we saw hatchlings making their way to the sea for the first time. Obviously, you can't plan for that, but it was truly fantastic.Just be aware that it is a long wait, both at the visitors centre and on the beach and there are no guarantees. Highly recommended.
title: Amazing experience!

body: We visited when staying at the nearby buckingham place which was walking distance to the watch. There is an information centre which tells you about the different turtles. When a turtle comes in (ours grounded at around 9.15 but can be any time) the staff wait for the turtle to be settled and laying before going to see the turtle laying her eggs. This was well organised and important as not to disturb the turtle. We were then taken in small groups to see the process. The guides were very informative and the donation was very reasonable at 1000 SLR per person. We have been turtle watching in other countries and felt the guides did a good job and clearly had the welfare of the turtles as their primary concern.This was a magical experience to stand on a wild Sri Lankan beach waves crashing around us, stars twinkling above and watching a huge green turtle lay her eggs.. Loved it
title: Wonderful experience to see the turtles

body: It was a wonderfull experience seeing the turtle lay her eggs and return to the sea. Waiting for her on the beach while she was digging and closing her nest was definetely worth it. Going back for more tonight!!!!!
title: turtley excellent

body: We were impressed that we came second to the turtles. Our guide would not let us near until he was happy the turtle was settled. The conservation was key but we witnessed a turtle digging her nest. Very much one of the highlights of the area and even sitting on the beach waiting for the guide to allow us to approach in the darkness with waves crashing was a worthwhile experience.be prepared for a walk. Much more conservation project than a tourist attraction. No frills.
title: Turtles come first

body: As a vet student passionate about the well-being of wildlife, I would never commend an organisation I thought would be detrimental to an animals welfare. The turtle conservation project is a extremely worthwhile project, not only for conservation, but for the sustainabilty of the local community too. The attraction is perfect for wildlife enthusiasts who will not only consider the turtles, but also the project as a whole. Okay, so there are a few issues still to iron out, but I'm pretty sure all projects do. I've read some past reviews on here, and it sounds like the key driver for the quality of experience depends on who is managing the project. At the moment, it is run to a very high quality, and the couple running it are obviously very passionate about creating a sustainable relationship with the locals, which will inevitably help the project develop and hopefully maintain a constant level of standards to keep both tourists and locals happy. If you want to just snap a photo of these beautiful creatures, go to a zoo. Its dark when you go, and you're not allowed flash, so I really wouldn't bother bringing your camera. Why would you want to look behind a lens the whole time anyway? There's a lot of waiting around too, but again, you shouldn't be going if you're not prepared to give up a little of your time to experience such a beautiful sight. If you're not happy with what you're experiencing (from any project you visit), instead of going home in disappointment why not ask questions and learn a little of what a project like this entails. Finally, dont forget its an Non Governmental Organisation - which means the only way this bit of beach can be protected and maintained for turtles, is from tourists visiting, donating and respecting these beautiful creatures.
title: Perfect for the wildlife enthusiast

body: We had arrived at 21 p.m. It was hard to find the place (we had our own car) but locals helped to find a way. It was early April and we saw three turtles laying their eggs on the beach. Seeing these creatures emerging from the see, slowly but consistently doing their work and then dissappearing in the ocean was one of the best experience in Sri Lanka. I advice you to take a red light torch if you have one in home. An organisation's employee should have it, but when we appeared at the place he hadn't have any and was using normal one, which aggarvated wathing the turtles (they are light sensitive, but barely see the red one).
title: Mistical experience

body: We arrived at 8.30pm and were greeted by a very nice volunteer, and were taken down to the beach where 20 other people were waiting. Within the group, people were very conscious not to disturb the turtles, there was no flash, no flashlight or phone. We were fortunate enough to see two turtles. One of them was lost about 40 meters away from the beach and quite distressed. I am pretty sure having all of us around her and hearing all our voices made it worse. After an hour it started pouring down and things got a bit chaotic with the locals running straight back to the center and volunteers and tourists running like chickens on the beach (no one could find the way back to the info center). I kept thinking that with a bigger crowd and in hatchling season, people would have caused enormous damage. There was a bit of an uneasy feeling between the local guides and volunteers, and we found it hard to see where the money actually goes. I guess the whole observation activity, when turned into a tourist attraction, becomes a danger for the wildlife. We both left with the same uncomfortable feeling (and that's before I actually read the shocking reviews on this page). If you really love the animals, maybe give this a pass.
title: Not sure this is the way

body: We got to Rekawa Turtle sanctuary at 8:30pm and we were met by a naturalist which our driver/guide had arranged for us. The naturalist was very knowledgeable and made the experience more interesting by explaining about Turtles and the conservation work being done at the sanctuary. We were taken down to the beach area, and there was a Greenback turtle already digging out an area to lay her eggs. You are not allowed to use torches, they have a red light which they use to watch the turtles so that they are not disturbed. The turle was flicking out sand, which flicked on us a bit, it was great. We then waited patiently on the sand banks and watched the clear night sky and gazed at the stars, it was really beautiful. We then went back to see the Turtle actually laying her eggs, it was really nice natural spectacle and any nature lover would love to see it. The experience ended after we watched the Turtle close up the nest and then head back out to the Ocean, definately worth a visit! You are best wearing flip flops for this experience, we wore trek boots, they got soaked when the tide came in over our feet!
title: a beautiful experience

body: Great experience of watching turtles lying eggs!!!! a little bit hard to find when you walk along the beach since there is noone to ask for directions, but after that well group organised and cheap (£4pp)
title: Turtle Watch :)

body: My boyfriend and I went along late at night and waited in the conservation area for about 3 hours before being taken down onto the beach. No-one spoke to us when we came in, and then we were only allowed on the beach about 20 minutes before being asked to come up again. We felt we didn't get a chance to lookout for turtles for very long. On the way back up from the beach the guide started asking us for money so he could afford to eat. We said he would put it in the donation box because that is what we always said we would do, and he started getting a bit funny with us. It's an awesome marine centre with lots of information and still worth a visit - whether you see a turtle or not.
title: Nice conservation centre, worth a visit

body: One of the main reasons for visiting this part of Sri Lanka was to visit the turtle conservation project. We were enthralled watching the turtle laying her eggs and returning to the ocean under a clear full moon. The staff were helpful and friendly and shared a deep knowledge and passion for their work.
title: A humbling experience.

body: We were lucky enough to see two green turtles on the night we visited but had to keep a good distance away from them so really only saw their silhouettes in the moonlight. It's a shame that the gentleman guiding us had very poor english and his research talk was somewhat lost in translation
title: a little dissappointing

body: Was there on the 01.03.2014. At first (20.30) we were only 4 people but then some more arrived and we were about 30 people. We waited (with some "false alarms") until 24.00 - then we saw a really big turtle, but she did not find a good spot for her nest so she went back to the sea. I still really liked the experience...being on the silent beach in the night with stars and so on... Also I talked a lot with the current "Program Manager" (from netherland) which is a really nice guy and knows what he's talking about! Fortunately our group was quiet and sticked to the rules :) all in all I can recommend it and I think it's a goood thing to support. But keep in mind: this ist not for everyone, there is no touching and maybe also not much seeing (so it may be not a place for children which don't understand it)...but if you are into nature and wildlife you should come :)
title: Nice experience

body: Really loved this experience. One of nature´s finest and I wish the project all the best. Unfortunatelly there were a bit too many tourist when we were there and the one guide let the people a bit too close to the animals in my opinion. I´m no turtle expert but it seemed like it stressed the turtle. Don´t expect good photos since it´s dark and there is only red light but therefore it will be a great memory for life. It takes time so be prepared to stay there several hours. Some French people were complaing that they could have spent their time and money better in Mirissa so I guess it´s not the place for everyone...
title: Magic moment

body: a lonely protected beach where 5 species of sea turtles (including the huge leatherback) come on land to leg their eggs. You have there to be at eight when they open. In a small but very informative information centre you can learn a lot about sea turtles, their life circle and their protection. Meanwhile guides on the beach will look for turtles on land to brig you close to them when they started to lay their eggs.We were there in the wrong season (better is May/June), we knew that, so we were not dissapointed to much, when we finally did not see a single turtle - you get your money back in that case anyway.The problem is: there are too many tourist (mainly Frensh for some odd reason), and too few guides: so when we finally went to the beach to wait for turtles - the group was too big and too loud, you are suppossed not to use your own torches, but the guides could not controll such a big group: so I fear that his will disturb the turtles if they come ashore. In the end we were kind of glad that no turtle showed up - all that noise and flashes of cameras would have upset us. (that had happened the night before, when a turtle finally had shown up)Summary : a great place to go and see wild life, if they only could manage to controll the crowd!
title: great place to see turtles but they can't manage the crowd yet

body: This project has competent turned around from what I understand and there are 4 or 5 volunteers now running the show helping to conserve the turtles natural environment and keep them safe. Friendly staff, great knowledge and a very worthy cause. Seeing a large green turtle laying her eggs on the beach was definitely a highlight of our Sri Lanka trip. Thanks again!
title: Great experience, not to be missed

body: Having read some of the negative reviews, our experience was completely the polar opposite.We were greeted by a young English couple who after explaining the process, took us down to the beach to wait quietly. We were told that if and when a turtle came ashore, we would be asked to move slightly closer (70 to 100m) away and wait patiently for her to lay her eggs. Only then were we allowed to approach her in small groups, as it happened on the night a green turtle tried to build an egg chamber but the sand was too soft so she abandoned her nest. We were told we could approach her as she headed back to the sea at a safe distance in order not to disturb her. We were not allowed to use flash or torches and were absolutely delighted to see this wonderful animal.The locals patrol the beaches 24x7 to protect egg stealing - funded by the visitors to TCP!! so keep visiting, they need the money!Tip - take water as you maybe there for a while!Karl & Dawn, Staffordshire, England.
title: Great Experience!

body: After reading all the negative reviews on Tripadvisor, I was expecting my turtle watching trip to be a rip-off. But I was pleasantly surprised to find it otherwise.As per David, who is volunteering as the project lead, the NGO which had started the project lost its source of funds and had to shut down the operations last year. That was when they handed over the operations to the local people, who hardly spoke English. And that was when all the negative reviews on Tripadvisor came in since the locals could not explain anything about the turtles' nesting behaviors to the tourists and the only interaction with them was when they asked for the turtle watching fees, which is a legitimate fee that pays for the salaries of the people manning the beach against predators poaching the turtle eggs.David and his team of volunteers (which included a marine biologist from the UK) were extremely friendly and they explained a lot of things to us about turtles, their life-cycle, nesting behavior and the threats to the survival of the species. We were fortunate to find a turtle the night we went. Although according to David, at least one turtle has been spotted every day since May 2013. So the chances of seeing turtles are pretty good. At the time the turtle was digging her nest and the egg chamber, we were asked to wait far away from her so as not to scare her away. And then when she was finally laying her eggs, were we allowed to go up close (albeit out of her line of sight). We used red LED lights since red light happens to fall outside the turtles' visible spectrum (meaning they cannot see red light).The overall tour was very smooth, professional and informative. I would strongly recommend it.
title: Wonderful Experience

body: I had really wanted to go to see turtles but was wary after reading some older reviews. I decided to go and am so glad I did, it was the highlight of my trip. The project is under new management and is a true conservation project now. There are 2 marine biologists on staff which are incredibly wonderful. They gave a information talk before we went to the beach and explain the beach "rules" - ie no flashlights other than the guides because red light doesn't bother them but all other types do, no smoking on the beach, no getting to close or touching the turtles, and no flash photography. We were able to see a female green turtle during her laying process then backed off while she covered her nest. When she was ready to go we were able to follow her as she made her way back to the ocean. While there was some waiting it was such a beautiful night and the beach is lovely so really I found it to be a great experience. I would recommend anyone who is at all interested in turtles (and has a little patience) not to miss this wonderful beach.
title: Under new management and its FANTASTIC

body: Before coming to Sri Lanka I really wanted to go turtle watching, and I had planned to visit the TCP (turtle conservation project) at Rekawa but then read some of the bad reviews on here. After a couple indicating that the project was getting better in terms of conservation, I tentatively decided to go and decide for myself.I had a great evening, there were several European volunteers who are friendly and knowledgeable about the turtles. The setup is that the visitors wait at the information centre until the volunteers get a call from the volunteers patrolling the beach. When they spot a turtle, you go down to the beach and wait for the turtle to start laying eggs, as this is when she is least easily disturbed. Only red lights are allowed and absolutely no camera flashes etc are permitted. The volunteers are always watching for signs that the turtle is distressed and at any sign they will make the visitors back off and switch off the lights. The priority was to let the turtle lay her eggs undisturbed which I thought was spot on.We were very lucky to see a baby loggerhead turtle scrambling towards the sea and a green turtle nesting on the beach. I stayed until 1.30am so make sure you are feeling refreshed when the evening begins and bring water/snacks if you wish.
title: Turned over a new leaf - and the result is excellent

body: When we came to Sri Lanka seeing turtles was high on our priority list. We read about the project in the Lonely Planet Guidebook and we came to Tangalla specifically to try and see turtles. Being nature lovers I think if we'd read some of the reviews below beforehand we wouldn't have come but I'm so glad we did. Upon arriving after a long and dark tuk tuk ride down a very bumpy track (No need for alarm, it does lead to the TCP visitor centre!) were were greeted with a big friendly welcome by the European volunteers. They were all very knowledgeable. They explained that things had come a bit out of hand in the past two years but early in 2013 a new project manager had taken over, strict rules put in place and non disturbing observation made a priority. At 8.30 the resident Marine Biologists give a talk on turtle biology and conservation. Make sure you get there early to ask lots of questions as they knew plenty about other marine life too! After the introduction in their new visitor centre they took our money (1000rs) but told us if we didn't see a turtle we were welcome to ask for it back. We then headed down to the beach to sit on the moonlit sand and await the arrival of a turtle. When one of the local guides had spotted a turtle we were escorted closer but kept well back until she had begun to lay. Only the volunteers and guides were allowed to use torches which were all red light only. We were allowed to take photos but only without flash - I'd recommend bringing a small tripod if you have one.Overall it was a great experience. The staff were very knowledgeable, kept us well back until it was safe to approach and we were really very impressed with their attitude. There was a lot of waiting around on the beach (We didn't leave until 11.30) and nothing is rushed so make sure you bring some water. Hopefully TCP Rekawa will carry on with its improved experience.Visited June 2013
title: A fresh start and awesome experience!

body: Having read the reviews and also spoken to the owner of the local hotel we were very concerned about going. However we met the new head volunteer on our way back from a day time visit to the beach and were delighted to hear how he has been asked to make sure this becomes a consistently high standard and improved event. We turned up at 20.30 with an open mind. There were clear instructions as to what to expect, no use of any torches by visitors and the volunteers were only using red light torches so as not to disturb the turtles. We were not able to go near the turtle until she had started laying and were asked to keep very silent. An incredible animal who after 2 hours of preparing her nest, laying and covering the eggs returned to the surf. Everything was well managed and we sincerely expect this to be a more regular review in the future knowing the efforts being put in place to raise the standards. Yes, there is work to do and they do need more funding in order to put in place the plans that the head volunteer has in mind, but we sensed this is very much on the right path. A truly memorable evening.
title: Delighted with the evening

body: Think I must have been there the same night as Alee101 and steffip89. Their reviews sum it all up really.This is not conservation in the slightest. I left the beach feeling very uncomfortable about what I had just witnessed.Please do not go as the people there are obviously just after profit now.If you do feel the need to go please do not take bright torches, the turtles were obviously distressed and confused.
title: 100% not conservation

body: We arrived at the beach at around 8 and waited 2 hours to see the first turtle. When we did see one it was a very depressing experience. About 50 tourists were standing around this poor turtle many of whom were using their own torches. One person had an incredibly bright head lamp and this was visibly distressing the animal. Not surprisingly, the two turtles we saw were unable to lay eggs.
title: Give this a miss

body: We went to the turtle sanctuary and it was a very sad experience. They really don't actually take care of the animal- they just want to see ur money. When we were there there were about 40 tourists. At the beginning a belgian girl introduced us to the site but claimed that she was doing a social study and had no proper knowledge about turtles. After some while a turtle came, but was obviously disturbed by the massive amount of tourists. While it was supposed to dig its whole in the sand the Belgian girl already came to ask for money with a local. becuase now it was gonna be for sure that we gonna see a turtle. Suddenly one of the locals ran to the tourist group and told us to run after the turtle to see it, becuase it was going back in the water. Suddenly 40 tourists where after that poor turtle and made pictures, used their torches... but no local naturalist seemed to care. After that we were told there was another turtle on the other end of the beach. Same story again: turtle intended to lay eggs but was then scared off by the people. But when it wanted to go back in the water this time, the locals stopped it from walking back in the water by yelling at it, pointing light on it and blocking it's way. Is this a real way of watching animals? They just wanted the tourists too see the turtle , so they wouldn't need to refund the money. A few tourists haven't seen the first turtle so they needed to be satisfied.After telling the begian girl afterwards that I don't think they treat the turtles in a nice way, she just answered very snappy: I am against tourist observation of animals. What?? How does that make sense? Why is she helping the locals to do such a cruel thing? A lot of other people where also disturbed by what happened there and I hope that YOU now decide not to stop by at this place during your trip.
title: no conservationists - again just a tourist rip off

body: I agree 100% with Henry Trafalgar's commentsWell, let me start by saying that I have seen turtle nesting before, actually my wife and I saw it in Oman almost 1 month before coming to Sri Lanka. With a beautiful experience fresh in mind we decided to go to Rewake beach to see it again.We took the long tuk tuk ride to get there. When we arrived we found a whole bunch of morons conducting what they call TCP. Also we found another bunch of morons, the tourist present that night, especially the Russians that did not speak any English and some of them even took off to find turtles by themselves.When they found the first turtle they asked us to go to take a look.... a good surprise the turtle was going back to the sea because they had disturbed it and could not lay the eggs. People starting taking photos using flash even though the "conservation guy" told them not to.The turtle went back to the sea. We were told to go to the other end of the beach to see anther turtle and at that time they started asking for money. I decided to confront the "TCP employees" and I told them that I will not give my money until they got control of the situation and make people respect the turtles. I even explained what I had learned in Oman. The discussion was long and did not go anywhere..... they do not understand and never will. They are just uneducated village people, not naturalists. I have been trying to contact Thushan Kapurusinghe, the "clown" director of TCP, to voice my concern but I have not been able to find an e-mail address.Other people also left because they did not agree to what was happening.If you want to do something good for these beautiful animals, PLEASE DO NOT GO TO SEE IT HERE, there are other places in the world where it can be seen and that takes care of the turtles. Go to Oman, a great country with wonderful people and a great project for turtle conservation. In July and August you can see 80 to 100 turtles nesting every night.
title: Please do not go. Awful experience.....money grabbers!
Great moonlight walk! Be charged up.
body: We went on a full moon poya night. Obviously others thought it was a great idea too so we had quite. Crowd of around 30 people. The moonlight walk on the beach is really nice and worth an experience. We arrived there by tuk tuk from tangalla which is abt 25 mins away. The road gets rough towards the end but its not terrible. Anyway we expected to be there for an hour but ended up being there for 2 hours! Still, understandably one cannot predict when the turtles will come. Thushara, reverse baseball cap, is a good resource. He is the main guy there and is quite friendly. Pls be warned that you must take water and be prepared to wait so be adequately charged up especially with kids. Take a torchlight and be prepared to walk on the beach to get to turtle. Take a torch. unfortunately we had to leave so didn't see the turtle but others said they did. Price is 1000 to see turtle but if u don't then u get a refund. The moonlight walk is priceless!

title: Ignorant money grabbers, not naturalists. Rip off.
body: We spent three nights waiting for turtles, so I suppose you could say that of all the reviews on this site, we're veterans.Based at the Amanwella in Tangalle, this was promoted as a local attraction. It sounded superb, we waited until the hotel got the call from the TCP guys on the beach letting us know that there was a turtle laying. We then made the mad dash to the beach, the last 4 km being off the Tarmac, bouncy!When we got there, there were about 25 or 30 people already there, looking disconsolate. All were talking loudly, most had torches. Most were dressed in bright beach or holiday type colours.I have done a great deal of stalking and wildfowling. Wild nocturnal animals HATE torches. They HATE the sound of the human voice. They avoid people.The turtle had done a u-turn and gone back to the sea.What a joke. The reversed-baseball-capped village boy taking the money rushed up to us and demanded money.This happened for 3 nights. The last night we did see a poor hounded turtle rushing (at 0.5mph) back to safety in the sea.The boys from our hotel, who had been turtle watching for 15 years on this beach, said that since the old Englishman, Richard, who started the project years ago, had "gone" a few months ago, the thing had totally degenerated into a wildlife disaster and money grabbing rip off.Sad.

title: A memorable experience
body: Amazing experience and so reasonably (1000 R). Got the call from our tuk tuk driver that there was a turtle on the beach at 9 pm. We were staying in Tangalle, so it took about 30 min to get there and then we had to walk about 20 min on the beach. The turtle had just finished laying its eggs when we got there and was slowly covering the hole. Surreal to watch and the stars out there were amazing too. The staff seemed fairly respective of the turtle, although they do use regular flashlights (in Costa Rica, they use special red flashlights). The whole process takes awhile, so be prepared to be there for over an hour. As the turtle was making its way back to the beach, one of the guides did try to get my daughter to touch the shell, which I objected to. A great experience and I would definitely recommend it.

title: A bit of a con
body: Firstly Rekawa is not in North Western Province. It is in the Southern Province near Tangalle. We were disappointed in the casual approach of the nature wardens apparently running the exercise. There is a long tuk tuk journey from Tangalle ending in a very rough and uncomfortable ride on local tracks. We had an informative chat from one of the western project workers which was good. The locals who are supposed to be policing it stood around chatting loudly (we were all told to be quiet!) After about 2 hours, we did eventually see a turtle which was heading back to the sea - we suspect put off laying by all the noise from the wardens. We then forked out 1200 rupees each (instead of the proclaimed 600) with no receipt and no record of where it was going. OK, we did see a turtle but we were distinctly unimpressed by the set up.

title: An amazing experience
body: What a surprise. Compared to the whale watching at Mirissa, Turtle watching is under-hyped in Sri Lanka. But it's incredibly worth it! A pleasant night waiting under the stars while the locals patrolled the beach, then when a turtle appeared we were able to go and watch while it laid about 100 eggs! Then we watched this giant prehistoric beast cover the nest, then drag its massive bulk back down to the sea. We could get really close and we saw everything! The only recommendation is that you make sure you pay the locals directly on the beach. The night we were there, there was some unpleasantness when a local person obviously had a deal going on with some tourists, and he didn't want them to pay on the beach, saying 'tomorrow, tomorrow'. It was clear that maybe tomorrow wouldn't come, and it was awkward for the other tourists, who wanted their money to go to the conservation effort.
